18	arXiv:2507.22659v2 [cs.SE] 19 Dec 2025
19	                                         The increasing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in software engineering has sparked interest in
20	                                         their use for software vulnerability detection. However, the rapid development of this field has resulted in a
21	                                         fragmented research landscape, with diverse studies that are difficult to compare due to differences in, e.g.,
22	                                         system designs and dataset usage. This fragmentation makes it difficult to obtain a clear overview of the state-of-
23	                                         the-art or compare and categorize studies meaningfully. In this work, we present a comprehensive systematic
24	                                         literature review (SLR) of LLM-based software vulnerability detection. We analyze 263 studies published
25	                                         between January 2020 and November 2025, categorizing them by task formulation, input representation, system
26	                                         architecture, and techniques. Further, we analyze the datasets used, including their characteristics, vulnerability
27	                                         coverage, and diversity. We present a fine-grained taxonomy of vulnerability detection approaches, identify
28	                                         key limitations, and outline actionable future research opportunities. By providing a structured overview of
29	                                         the field, this review improves transparency and serves as a practical guide for researchers and practitioners
30	                                         aiming to conduct more comparable and reproducible research. We publicly release all artifacts and maintain
31	                                         a living repository of LLM-based software vulnerability detection studies at https://github.com/hs-esslingen-
32	                                         it-security/Awesome-LLM4SVD.
33	                                         Additional Key Words and Phrases: Software Vulnerability Detection, Vulnerability Detection, Software
34	                                         Engineering, Vulnerability Datasets, Benchmark Datasets, LLM, SLR, Survey
35	
36	                                         1   Introduction
37	                                         Vulnerability detection plays a critical role in the software development life cycle, identifying
38	                                         security vulnerabilities before they can be exploited in deployed systems. The growing complexity of
39	                                         modern software, combined with an ever-increasing threat landscape, has led to a surge in reported
40	                                         vulnerabilities. The Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) records [46] provide unique
41	                                         identifiers for publicly known software vulnerabilities. Over 40,000 CVEs have been published in
42	                                         2024 alone, with over 12,000 reported in the first quarter of 2025 [45]. Complementing CVEs, the
43	                                         Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) [213] offers a hierarchical classification of vulnerability
44	                                         types, serving as a higher-level abstraction for understanding underlying vulnerability patterns.
45	                                            Vulnerability assessment pipelines as found in industrial development workflows typically
46	                                         consist of multiple steps: detection (identifying whether code contains a vulnerability), localization
47	                                         (pinpointing the exact location in the code), severity estimation (evaluating potential impact), and
48	                                         repair (patching the code to mitigate the vulnerability), often initiated reactively when a new CVE
49	                                         is disclosed. Despite advances in tooling, e.g., static application security testing (SAST) tools, these
50	                                         processes remain largely manual or only partially automated due to the dependency on expert-
51	                                         defined rules (cf. Taghavi and Feyzi [304] for a comparison between LLMs and established software
52	                                         vulnerability detection methods). Further, these tools suffer from high false positive rates [42]. As
53	                                         such, existing workflows are insufficient to meet the scale of remediation demands.
54	                                         Authors’ Contact Information: Sabrina Kaniewski, sabrina.kaniewski@hs-esslingen.de, Esslingen University, Esslingen,
55	                                         Germany; Fabian Schmidt, fabian.schmidt@hs-esslingen.de, Institute for Intelligent Systems, Esslingen University, Esslingen,
56	                                         Germany; Markus Enzweiler, markus.enzweiler@hs-esslingen.de, Institute for Intelligent Systems, Esslingen University,
57	                                         Esslingen, Germany; Michael Menth, menth@uni-tuebingen.de, Chair of Communication Networks, University of Tübingen,
58	                                         Tübingen, Germany; Tobias Heer, tobias.heer@hs-esslingen.de, Esslingen University, Esslingen, Germany.
59	
60	=== [PDF page 2] ===
61	
62	2                                                                                                    Kaniewski et al.
63	
64	
65	   At the same time, the adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs)1 for software engineering
66	tasks has grown rapidly since the introduction of BERT [53] in 2018. LLMs are deep neural net-
67	work models, typically based on Transformer architectures [323], that are pre-trained on massive
68	corpora of natural language. LLMs have demonstrated impressive capabilities in understanding
69	and generating code. Industry forecasts further emphasize the transformative potential of LLMs in
70	code generation [10].
71	   However, while LLMs hold promise in code generation, they also introduce new risks. Generated
72	code often lacks awareness of existing libraries or internal codebases, which may lead to redundan-
73	cies and the creation of syntactically different but semantically equivalent code. This complicates
74	the detection of vulnerabilities, especially when they are subtle or semantically nuanced. Addi-
75	tionally, LLMs are prone to hallucinations and the generation of insecure code [84, 181, 188, 242].
76	Development teams may be unaware of vulnerabilities introduced by generated code, whether in
77	their codebase, third-party components, or libraries.
78	   The combination of LLM-generated code and the increasing volume of vulnerabilities calls for
79	automated, scalable, and reliable vulnerability assessment pipelines. LLMs’ ability to generalize
80	across programming languages and representations, as well as their high flexibility through prompt
81	adaptation, make them a promising approach for software vulnerability assessment. Therefore,
82	recent research has begun to explore the use of LLMs. In a prior study [143], we surveyed early work
83	on LLM-based vulnerability handling, including detection, localization, and repair, and highlighted
84	open challenges with regard to scalability, data diversity, and model reliability. We continued to
85	extensively document the progress in this field, with a focus on vulnerability detection studies
86	as a prerequisite for all subsequent remediation steps. As the number of studies on LLM-based
87	vulnerability detection continues to grow, we observe a wide variety of system architectures,
88	adaptation techniques, and evaluation methodologies. This heterogeneity leads to two pressing
89	challenges: First, there is currently no comprehensive survey that maps the landscape of
90	LLM-based software vulnerability detection methods, their system designs, and dataset usage.
91	As a result, researchers face difficulties identifying trends, gaps, or best practices in this
92	rapidly evolving area. Second, studies frequently adopt custom datasets, metrics, and data
93	splits, making it difficult to assess progress, reproduce results, or compare models fairly.
94	To address these challenges, we contribute this systematic literature review (SLR) of LLM-based
95	software vulnerability detection studies. Specifically, our contributions are as follows:
96	      • We conduct a SLR of studies covering LLM-based software vulnerability detection in the
97	        time from January 2020 to November 2025, covering 263 studies.
98	      • We present a comprehensive taxonomy that categorizes existing approaches based on
99	        task formulation (classification and generation), input representation (code and auxiliary
100	        information), system architecture (LLM usage), adaptation and orchestration technique, as
101	        well as dataset usage. This taxonomy allows for meaningful comparison of studies.
102	      • We perform an in-depth analysis of commonly used and selected datasets, investigat-
103	        ing class balance, CWE coverage as well as diversity, and limitations. Based on this analysis,
104	        we provide actionable insights and best practices for future dataset selection and evaluation
105	        design to improve cross-study comparability.
106	      • We discuss overarching limitations and challenges of current LLM-based vulnerability
107	        detection approaches and outline future research opportunities.

129	2 Related Work
130	With the growing adoption of LLMs across various domains, numerous works have emerged to
131	explore their applications. In this section, we discuss related works, covering related SLRs and
132	surveys that intersect most closely with the topic of LLM-based software vulnerability detection,
133	as well as works focusing on vulnerability datasets.
134	
135	2.1   Related SLRs and Surveys
136	In Table 1, we provide an overview of related surveys, with particular attention to their coverage
137	of the main aspects of this SLR, i.e., focus on LLM-based studies, input representations, adaptation
138	techniques, analysis of datasets, and a comprehensive taxonomy. In the following, we discuss these
139	surveys and how this SLR differs in coverage from previous works.
140	   Several surveys analyze the application of LLMs in the domain of cyber security [75, 357],
141	addressing vulnerability detection as one of several sub-tasks. Xu et al. [357], for example, cover
142	the domains of software and system security, network security, information and content security,
143	hardware security, and blockchain security. The authors focus on what LLMs have been employed
144	to support these security tasks, and discuss domain-specific adaptation techniques, i.e., fine-tuning,
145	prompt engineering, and external augmentation. Further, they address dataset collection and
146	pre-processing techniques. Ferrag et al. [75] focus on LLMs employed for cyber security and
147	their optimization strategies, briefly discussing advanced training and fine-tuning techniques. The
148	authors also provide an overview of software vulnerability datasets used for fine-tuning.
149	   Surveys in the domain of software engineering [80, 114, 380] categorize LLM usage by
150	phases of the software development life cycle. Vulnerability detection is typically part of software
151	testing [380] or software quality assurance [114]. Fu et al. [80] focus on AI for DevSecOps, covering
152	software vulnerability detection and classification. Due to the broader scope of AI, the survey
153	covers fewer studies applying LLM. Zhang et al. [380] focus on the LLM perspective, providing a
154	comprehensive overview of code LLMs, discussing pre-training tasks, and downstream applications.
155	Hou et al. [114] discuss techniques used to optimize LLMs, including prompt engineering and fine-
156	tuning techniques. The authors also provide an overview of input forms used for diverse software
157	engineering tasks (i.e., token- and tree/graph-based) and highlight data collection, selection, and pre-
158	processing processes. While these surveys provide overviews of the application of LLMs in broader
159	domains, we focus on insights into the state-of-the-art adaptation and orchestration techniques,
160	input representations, and datasets that are specific to software vulnerability detection.

164	deep learning specific input (tree, graph, token) [282, 285] or program representations (source,
165	binary, intermediate) [279] and provide an overview of common datasets. Shimmi et al. [282] also

259	2.2    Vulnerability Datasets
260	A further distinguishing aspect of this SLR from previous surveys is its in-depth analysis of
261	vulnerability detection datasets. High-quality, realistic, and diverse datasets play a crucial role
262	in learning-based software vulnerability detection, prompting studies to analyze, classify, and
263	evaluate their characteristics, quality, and impact on model performance. Discussed surveys have
264	touched upon vulnerability detection datasets: Xu et al. [357] and Hou et al. [114] categorize
265	dataset collection, i.e., open-source, collected, constructed, or industrial, as well as dataset type, i.e.,
266	code-based, text-based, graph-based, software repository-based, or combined. Shiri Harzevili et
267	al. [285] categorize dataset sources into benchmark, hybrid, open source software, and repository.
268	Further, they differentiate code, text, numerical, and hybrid dataset types. Shereen et al. [279]
269	compare frequently used datasets with respect to properties such as language, size, annotation,
270	and granularity. Similarly, other discussed surveys [75, 80, 89, 277, 282, 304] list used datasets with
271	respect to, e.g., size, programming language, granularity, or source. In contrast to previous surveys
272	that primarily list datasets, we present a taxonomy and comprehensive analysis. We categorize
273	datasets along type, granularity, source, and labeling methodology, and investigate additional
274	quality dimensions, such as class balance, CWE diversity, and distribution, offering an in-depth
275	analysis of represented vulnerabilities. Further, we add a time component and discuss emerging
276	trends and use cases for datasets in LLM-based software vulnerability detection.
277	   Other related studies focus explicitly on vulnerability detection datasets: Hu et al. [116] analyze
278	benchmarks for evaluating LLM-based solutions, focusing on construction methods, programming
279	languages, and metrics. Lin et al. [179] examine dataset construction methodologies, comparing
280	datasets across six dimensions, such as granularity, vulnerability type, and labeling approach.
281	Guo et al. [101] analyze selected datasets in terms of vulnerability distributions and types. Jain et
282	al. [127] provide a code-centric evaluation of commonly used C/C++datasets for deep learning-based
283	vulnerability detection. Moreover, the works [42, 100, 264, 360] provide in-depth analyses of quality
284	issues in selected vulnerability datasets, such as data imbalance, low vulnerability coverage, biased
285	vulnerability distribution, high duplication rates, and label noise. Despite this growing body of work,
286	a targeted and comprehensive overview of vulnerability detection datasets commonly used for
287	LLM-based software vulnerability detection approaches, along with their limitations and suitability,
288	remains missing. This survey addresses this gap, offering a taxonomy and systematic analysis of
289	datasets, their CWE coverage, diversity, and usage, thereby facilitating better comparability and
290	benchmarking in future research.

292	3     Methodology
293	We followed established guidelines by Kitchenham et al. [150, 246] for conducting SLRs in software
294	engineering, i.e., defining research questions, conducting the search, defining selection criteria, and
295	analyzing the selected studies. In the following, we outline the research focus of this SLR as well as
296	the three phases of literature search, study selection, and study analysis, as visualized in Figure 1.
297	
298	3.1    Research Focus
299	In this SLR, we address the following research questions RQ1–RQ5:

305	
306	    RQ1 How is the vulnerability detection task formulated and approached in LLM-based
307	        systems? Traditional deep-learning-based approaches predominantly frame the detection
308	        task as binary classification (vulnerable vs. non-vulnerable) [279]. While this formulation
309	        simplifies evaluation, it falls short in reflecting real-world software engineering work-
310	        flows, where developers additionally require information on, e.g., vulnerability types and
311	        root causes. As LLMs are capable of producing structured reasoning steps and conceptual
312	        explanations, understanding whether LLM-based approaches move beyond this limited
313	        formulation is essential. We investigate how existing LLM-based approaches formulate the
314	        task, i.e., do they maintain the binary framing or do they extend or reformulate it, e.g., as
315	        multi-label vulnerability type prediction or vulnerability report generation (cf. Section 4.1).
316	    RQ2 How is input, particularly the semantics of vulnerabilities, represented and en-
317	        coded for LLMs? Existing machine learning and deep learning approaches convert code
318	        into suitable representations to capture semantics, for example, by constructing graph
319	        structures for GNNs or vectorizing code embeddings for CNNs [279, 285]. For LLMs with
320	        their world knowledge, it remains unclear whether code alone is sufficient to capture spe-
321	        cific vulnerability semantics. Investigating how studies represent input and whether they
322	        incorporate auxiliary information is crucial to understanding what information LLMs can
323	        leverage for effective detection (cf. Section 4.2).
324	    RQ3 What are the predominant techniques for adapting LLMs to the task of software
325	        vulnerability detection? LLMs can be adapted via prompting, fine-tuning, or pre-training.
326	        Each technique has different implications for data requirements, computational costs, and
327	        practical deployment. Since these constraints affect the feasibility of integrating LLM-based
328	        methods into software engineering pipelines, this question investigates which adaptation
329	        techniques are used and how well they align with practical constraints (cf. Section 4.4.2).
330	    RQ4 What datasets are used to train, tune, or evaluate LLM-based vulnerability detection
331	        approaches, and how does dataset selection impact applicability? Dataset selection
332	        influences the types and variety of vulnerabilities under detection. In terms of applicability,
333	        synthetic or oversimplified datasets lead to models with poor generalization. Therefore,
334	        understanding the characteristics (such as covered vulnerability types, size, and label quality)
335	        of the datasets used in current research is essential to enable reliable benchmarking and
336	        assess model generalization to real-world applications (cf. Section 5).
337	    RQ5 How does dataset selection impact comparability across studies? Dataset selection
338	        influences whether results are comparable across studies. Inconsistent evaluation setups as
339	        well as not adhering to open science practices make it impossible to compare study results.
340	        Identifying commonly used datasets as part of evaluation setups enables researchers to
341	        select datasets to improve comparability across studies (cf. Section 5.3).
342	
343	   A joint investigation of RQ1-RQ5 is crucial to obtain a holistic understanding of LLM-based
344	vulnerability detection research, from input representations to system design and evaluation, and
345	to identify key levers to enhance robustness, practicability, and comparability.

347	3.2     Literature Search
348	To identify relevant studies, we conducted a systematic literature search across three major
349	databases: IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and arXiv. We selected IEEE Xplore and the ACM
350	Digital Library, as they host peer-reviewed publications from conferences and journals. We further
351	include arXiv for preprints to capture ongoing research that is still in the submission process, given
352	the rapidly evolving nature of this field.

376	3.3   Study Selection
377	Figure 1 illustrates the study selection pipeline used in this SLR. Using the final search string, we
378	ran an automated search across the selected databases to identify studies whose titles or abstracts
379	matched the specified keywords. We carried out the initial search in December 2024. After the
380	initial crawl, we continuously integrated newly published material through database-specific search
381	alerts and scholar.inbox [77], ensuring that further relevant studies were considered and included.
382	   Following this automated search, we applied a selection process to filter out irrelevant studies
383	based on predefined inclusion (✓) and exclusion (✗) criteria, cf. Table 2. We retrieved each accessible
384	study written in English and first filtered by title and abstract before performing a full text screen to
385	assess if it is in scope. Specifically, we focus on studies that apply LLMs to actively detect software
386	vulnerabilities, rather than applying LLMs to work with outputs of other detection tools, e.g.,
387	SAST tools. Further, we specifically focus on software vulnerability detection rather than detection
388	in binary code, smart contracts, network logs, or detection of malware. We further exclude any
389	duplicates or minor variations of multi- or extended-version papers as well as studies classified as
390	reviews, surveys, theses, abstracts, posters, demonstrations, or tutorials.
391	   Given the inclusion of preprints from arXiv, we conducted a manual quality assessment to deter-
392	mine study eligibility. We assessed whether the studies provided a clear contribution, adequately
393	described the proposed workflow and implementation, outlined the evaluation setup (including
394	datasets, baselines, and metrics), and presented coherent findings that support their central claims.
395	   After filtering, we performed backward and forward snowballing. We manually reviewed the
396	reference lists of the selected studies (backward snowballing) and used citation tracking via Google
397	Scholar to identify additional papers citing the included studies (forward snowballing). Studies
398	retrieved through snowballing also pass through the pipeline of inclusion and exclusion criteria.
399	   Finally, at the time of writing this SLR, we cover 263 studies. Further studies added through the
400	continuous search will be made available as part of the maintained repository, cf. [144].

533	4                 Vulnerability Detection with LLMs
534	Recent research has adopted a variety of techniques for detecting software vulnerabilities using
535	LLMs. In this chapter, we present a comprehensive taxonomy that categorizes the different ways
536	LLMs are applied to vulnerability detection. Specifically, we examine task formulations, input
537	representations, system architectures, and techniques. The overall taxonomy is illustrated in
538	Figure 3. We discuss each category on the basis of the surveyed studies in the following subsections.
539	
540	4.1                      Task Formulation (F)
541	Software vulnerability detection can be framed in multiple ways, depending on how the task is
542	formulated and what objectives are prioritized beyond detection (e.g., explanation). With respect to
543	the objectives, the integration of LLMs into vulnerability detection introduces unique advantages
544	over traditional approaches. Unlike rule-based approaches, which require definitions of vulnerable
545	patterns, the language understanding capabilities of LLMs allow for highly flexible goal setting;
546	
547	=== [PDF page 10] ===
548	
549	10                                                                                                                           Kaniewski et al.
550	
551	
552	detection objectives can be refined or expanded, e.g., adding reasoning or vulnerability localization,
553	simply by adjusting natural language prompts. LLMs further have extensive pre-trained world
554	knowledge, such as software architecture patterns, programming language-specific constructs, and
555	broad cybersecurity concepts. Such domain knowledge is difficult to encode explicitly in traditional

616	
617	
618	tools or classical ML approaches, but serves as a versatile starting point for LLM-based detection.
619	In the following, we outline and discuss the most common detection task formulations used with
620	LLMs in the surveyed studies: classification and generation tasks.
621	4.1.1 Classification (F1). Vulnerability detection is most commonly formulated as a classification
622	problem, differentiating binary and multi-class forms. Binary Classification (F1.1) determines
623	whether a given code contains a security vulnerability or not (’Yes’/’No’). Vulnerability-Specific
624	Classification (F1.1.1) [279], as a refinement of the binary formulation, determines whether a given
625	code contains a specific vulnerability, represented, e.g., by CWE-ID. Multi-Class Classification
626	(F1.2) determines which specific type of vulnerability the given code contains (type prediction), often
627	using CWE-IDs as class labels. This formulation may use a given pre-defined list of vulnerability
628	types in a prompt engineering setting. Similarly, Multi-Label Classification (F1.3) aims to
629	determine any vulnerability types present in the code, recognizing that a code snippet may contain
630	multiple distinct vulnerabilities simultaneously.
631	   Binary classification (F1.1, 195 studies) simplifies the detection task as it is reduced to a decision
632	of whether a code sample is vulnerable or not. While this approach facilitates model training and
633	deployment, it lacks fine-grained insight into the specific type or cause of the vulnerability, limiting
634	its use in real-world vulnerability remediation.
635	   Vulnerability-specific classification (F1.1.1, 20 studies) is more targeted, which is valuable in
636	contexts with high-impact CWEs or regulatory compliance. However, it depends on curated datasets
637	and may struggle to generalize to related vulnerability types not present in the training data.
638	   Multi-class (F1.2, 61 studies) and multi-label (F1.3, 23 studies) classification provide the most
639	detailed perspective by distinguishing among various types of vulnerabilities. These formulations
640	align more closely with real-world vulnerability remediation, where identifying the exact nature
641	of a vulnerability is essential for vulnerability patching. However, these formulations introduce
642	additional complexity in both modeling and evaluation. Their effectiveness also depends heavily
643	on high-quality, CWE-labeled, and well-distributed datasets.
644	   Some studies combine or cascade these formulations. For example, a binary classifier may act as
645	a preliminary filter or router, forwarding likely vulnerable samples to a CWE-specific classifier for
646	further analysis [363].
647	4.1.2 Generation (F2). While classification is the primary formulation, it offers limited explana-
648	tions and insights into the root causes of vulnerabilities. Therefore, several studies extend the
649	scope of classification and leverage the language understanding and generation capabilities of
650	LLMs to generate additional outputs. This generative approach takes advantage of the model’s
651	flexibility, allowing researchers to request diverse detection outputs, such as reasoning chains or
652	fix suggestions, through simple natural language instructions. We categorize generative tasks as
653	(i) vulnerability description, (ii) root cause reasoning, and (iii) structured vulnerability report.
654	    Vulnerability Description (F2.1) focuses on generating a high-level natural language summary
655	or description of the specific detected vulnerability, providing developers with its context [31, 41,
656	69, 79, 85, 123, 125, 153, 160, 161, 178, 217, 270, 286, 290, 295, 306, 330, 339, 367, 368].
657	    Root Cause Reasoning (F2.2) moves beyond high-level descriptions to provide a code-level
658	justification or reasoning of the specific vulnerability and its root cause [3, 37, 59, 63, 68, 104, 126,
659	128, 145–147, 160, 168, 169, 172, 173, 185, 187, 201, 202, 210, 222, 228, 270, 273, 288, 293, 301, 322,
660	326, 334, 340, 343, 347–349, 364, 365, 399, 403]. However, the reliability of LLM-generated reasoning
661	remains under scrutiny. For instance, Steenhoek et al. [293] perform an error analysis on LLM
662	responses, demonstrating that the models struggle to reason about the code semantics relevant to
663	identifying vulnerabilities, especially subtle semantic differences caused by small textual changes.
664	Wen et al. [347] propose forward and backward reasoning, where forward reasoning aims to deduce
665	
666	=== [PDF page 12] ===
667	
668	12                                                                                              Kaniewski et al.
669	
670	
671	
672

674	the classification task with a generative task. Numbers in braces indicate the absolute count of unique studies
675	applying the task formulation; a single study may perform multiple tasks.
676	
677	
678	the causes of vulnerabilities, while backward reasoning seeks to understand the code changes
679	in the fixes. Their results show that LLMs can reason about vulnerabilities but often lack the
680	domain-specific knowledge required to effectively invoke such reasoning.
681	   Other approaches request a Structured Vulnerability Report (F2.3) [65, 86, 90, 139, 145, 146,
682	198, 222, 231, 243, 245, 276, 301, 321, 343, 348, 350, 355, 365, 371, 397, 399, 403]: Studies often
683	aggregate multiple predictive sub-tasks, such as vulnerability localization, severity estimation,
684	type justification, and repair fixes, into a single structured output (e.g., JSON, structured text,
685	or standardized static analysis formats [90]). For example, Zibaeirad and Vieira [403] prompt
686	models to generate a report containing the CWE-ID, fix suggestion, vulnerability severity, and
687	exploitability. Similarly, Yang et al. [365] structure the output to include the label, confidence score,
688	vulnerability type, and affected components. Zhou et al. [397] produce reports detailing function
689	names, namespaces, source/sink type, and dangerous parameter indices.
690	   These generative tasks reflect a broader shift in the role of LLMs from simple classifiers to
691	end-to-end vulnerability assistants that support developers interactively throughout the software
692	development life cycle. Figure 4 maps the relationships between classification and generation
693	tasks across the surveyed studies. Each node is annotated with the absolute number of studies
694	using that task formulation, providing a quantitative overview of the landscape. The flows further
695	visualize studies that combine classification with generative tasks. These combined tasks create
696	opportunities for multitask benchmarks that evaluate detection accuracy alongside, e.g., reasoning
697	quality, localization precision, and severity estimation, offering a more holistic perspective on
698	vulnerability remediation.
699	
700	4.2   Input Representation (I)
701	The representation of the input code and additional context plays a pivotal role in effective vul-
702	nerability detection. Distinct from traditional static analysis tools that require language-specific
703	rules, LLMs offer unique capabilities in how they process input. First, their extensive pre-trained
704	world knowledge allows them to interpret diverse input forms, e.g., code and natural language
705	instructions. This flexibility enables the processing of multi-language source code with varied
706	
707	=== [PDF page 13] ===
708	
709	A Systematic Literature Review on Detecting Software Vulnerabilities with Large Language Models          13
710	
711	
712	vulnerability types and auxiliary information within a unified framework. Second, their semantic
713	understanding allows LLMs to generalize; by reasoning about the input rather than matching fixed
714	vulnerable patterns, LLMs may identify rare or novel vulnerabilities. Considering these capabilities,
715	we categorize input representations along the code and auxiliary information axes.
716	
717	4.2.1 Code (I1). Raw (I1.1) input representations of code involve feeding source code directly
718	into the model during inference as plain text sequences (used by 139 studies). This approach relies
719	entirely on the model’s understanding and pre-learned knowledge of programming syntax to detect
720	vulnerable patterns. This representation is widely used for training or fine-tuning LLMs. However,
721	raw code inputs may struggle to capture the deeper semantics and context necessary for detecting
722	subtle or complex vulnerabilities. As such, this approach may underperform in scenarios requiring
723	precise reasoning about program logic, data flow, or code structure.
724	   Combining raw code with or expanding representations to Structured (I1.2) code enhances
725	the model’s understanding of code by capturing deeper syntactic and semantic structures of code
726	and vulnerabilities, thereby addressing the limitations of relying solely on textual patterns. Code
727	is transformed into graph-based or other structured formats that expose control flow, data flow,
728	and dependency relationships relevant to vulnerability semantics. Common graph representations
729	include Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) [3, 16, 138, 170, 344, 374, 381], specifically flattened [170]
730	or decomposed [381], Control Flow Graphs (CFGs) [85, 182, 193, 303, 379], Data Flow Graphs
731	(DFGs) [137, 190, 329, 372], forms of Program Dependency Graphs (PDGs) [62, 112, 193, 300, 353],
732	combining data and control dependencies, and Code Property Graphs (CPGs) [32, 73, 157, 162, 175,
733	183, 221, 225, 259, 374], which integrate multiple code views (AST, CFG, PDG). Some studies employ
734	composite or multi-layered graph structures that integrate several of the above [124, 125, 134,
735	180, 182, 193, 390, 391], which can outperform other graphs [384], or combine multiple modalities
736	including text, graphs, and visual representations [225].
737	   In addition to graph structures, other structured inputs aim to isolate semantically relevant
738	code regions, such as program or code slices [57, 117, 299, 313, 354, 398], chunks [105], or code
739	gadgets [37, 95, 103, 149, 163, 235, 236, 244, 247, 251, 254, 311, 388, 389]. Code gadgets, in particular,
740	consist of program statements that are semantically related to each other through data or control
741	dependencies [174], isolating vulnerability-relevant code regions. Other studies include program
742	traces, i.e., execution-aware code structure [56, 220]. Mächtle et al. [220] specifically build trace
743	gadgets, i.e., trace the code before slicing. By making structural and semantic dependencies explicit,
744	structure-aware representations enable models to reason more effectively about vulnerability-
745	related behaviors, especially those that span across the codebase or require understanding of
746	program logic and execution flow.
747	
748	4.2.2 Auxiliary Information (I2). To enhance the effectiveness of vulnerability detection, studies
749	move beyond source code by augmenting the input with auxiliary information, particularly in
750	prompt-engineering settings. This additional information provides the model with domain knowl-
751	edge or code context. We categorize this auxiliary information into (i) vulnerability information,
752	(ii) semantic artifacts, (iii) execution artifacts, and (iv) tool output.
753	    Vulnerability Information (I2.1) involves explicitly equipping the model with domain vulnera-
754	bility knowledge. Most commonly, studies include a pre-defined list of CWEs to the prompt to narrow
755	the classification scope [18, 24, 60, 83, 90, 169, 185, 273, 276, 293, 327, 355, 371] or provide labeled ex-
756	amples (few-shot settings) [31, 37, 55, 59, 72, 109, 139, 155, 170, 187, 190, 193, 201, 227, 232, 238, 270,
757	278, 286, 290, 319–321, 326, 349, 365, 368, 369, 382, 394, 395]. Other studies include more detailed vul-
758	nerability (CWE) definitions and descriptions [27, 63, 153, 173, 202, 217, 243, 284, 301, 322, 350, 399],
759	particularly as part of retrieval architectures, or full analysis reports [197].
760	
761	=== [PDF page 14] ===
762	
763	14                                                                                         Kaniewski et al.
764	
765	
766	   Semantic Artifacts (I2.2) focus on the high-level intent and functionality of the code, bridging
767	the gap between syntax and understanding. For example, studies provide natural language expla-
768	nations of the code functionality [86, 316], questions regarding the code’s behavior [128], explicit
769	descriptions of data sources and sinks [162], or code comments and docstrings [119].
770	   Execution Artifacts (I2.3) capture the behavior, structural dependencies, or runtime environ-
771	ment of the code. Studies enrich inference input with data and control dependencies, interpro-
772	cedural interactions, and environment constraints [3]. For instance, researchers include informa-
773	tion on callee functions [169, 301], dynamic execution signals such as unit test results [210], or
774	code-context [169, 172, 273], e.g., global variables, type declarations, and library imports. Data
775	flow analysis techniques are also used [170, 306, 364, 397], e.g., to extract dependencies from call
776	graphs [345].
777	   Tool Output (I2.4) augments the model context with the outputs of other tools, most commonly
778	SAST tools, allowing the LLM to interpret the static analysis findings to refine further predictions [18,
779	145, 219, 340, 365]. Yang et al. [365] inputs the results of other deep learning models (i.e., the
780	prediction probability) to inform the final classification.
781	
782	4.3   System Architecture (S)
783	Vulnerability detection systems using LLMs differ significantly in which and how models are
784	integrated into the overall system. Broadly, we categorize existing approaches into two groups:
785	LLM-centric systems, where the LLM serves as the main predictive component, and hybrid systems,
786	which integrate an LLM with other learning-based components.
787	
788	4.3.1 LLM (S1). In LLM-centric approaches, the LLM performs the core predictive tasks, such as
789	classification and reasoning. The model is typically adapted to the detection task through prompt
790	engineering or fine-tuning. Additional tools, such as SAST, only provide auxiliary information
791	rather than predictive signals. The surveyed studies employ a variety of LLMs with different
792	architectures, pre-training domains, and scales. In the following, we discuss LLMs within these
793	categories to categorize systems in more detail.
794	
795	    Model Architecture (S1.1). Most LLMs are based on the Transformer architecture, which includes
796	encoder and decoder modules with a self-attention mechanism. We follow other works and cate-
797	gorize the LLMs used in the surveyed studies into the three architectural groups (i) encoder-only,
798	(ii) encoder-decoder, and (iii) decoder-only, as introduced by Pan et al. [240].
799	      • Encoder-Only (S1.1.1) LLMs, e.g., models from the BERT [53] family (CodeBERT [74],
800	        GraphCodeBERT [97], RoBERTa [186], DistilBERT [272]), use only the encoder to encode
801	        the sentence and comprehend the relationships between words [240]. The encoder maps the
802	        input code into a fixed-size dense vector representation (embedding) that captures semantic
803	        relationships. In vulnerability detection, these models are typically adapted via fine-tuning
804	        by adding a classification head (e.g., a multi-layer perceptron) to output a probability score or
805	        class label. Alternatively, they function as frozen feature extractors, generating embeddings
806	        that serve as input for external classifiers.
807	      • Encoder-Decoder (S1.1.2) LLMs, e.g., T5 [257], CodeT5 [335, 337], or UniXcoder [96], use
808	        both the encoder and decoder module in a sequence-to-sequence framework [240]. The
809	        encoder maps the input code into a latent hidden-state representation, which the decoder
810	        uses to generate a target output sequence. For vulnerability detection, this architecture
811	        allows the task to be framed as text generation, where the input is the source code and
812	        the output is a generated text string, e.g., the label "vulnerable" or a natural language
813	        explanation.
814	
815	=== [PDF page 15] ===
816	
817	A Systematic Literature Review on Detecting Software Vulnerabilities with Large Language Models    15
818	
819	
820	     • Decoder-Only (S1.1.3) LLMs use only the decoder module, using auto-regressive mech-
821	       anisms to predict the next token in a sequence. The input, typically a prompt containing
822	       instructions and the code snippet, is processed sequentially, and the output is generated as
823	       a continuation of this input, enabling the generation of reasoning chains and structured
824	       vulnerability reports. Many state-of-the-art LLMs follow this architecture, e.g., the GPT fam-
825	       ily [22, 237, 256] and the Llama family [93, 317, 318]. Decoder-only LLMs are the dominant
826	       architecture used for vulnerability detection in the surveyed studies.
827	
828	  Pre-Training Domain (S1.2). Surveyed studies rely on LLMs from two main domains: general-
829	purpose LLMs and code LLMs. General-Purpose LLMs (S1.2.1) are pre-trained on natural lan-
830	guage corpora and tend to perform well on explanation-based or natural language-heavy tasks.
831	Examples from this domain are the BERT family, the GPT family, the Llama family, the Qwen
832	series [17, 255, 361], Gemma [309, 310], DeepSeek [48, 49], Mistral [131], Mixtral [132], Claude [11],
833	Gemini [308], and Phi [1, 129]. Code LLMs (S1.2.2) are pre-trained specifically on large-scale code
834	corpora for code-related tasks, enhancing performance on syntax-sensitive or program-structure-
835	aware tasks. Examples include CodeBERT [74], GraphCodeBERT [97], StarCoder [164, 191], UniX-
836	coder [96], the GPT-based Codex [33], CodeLlama [265], CodeQwen 1.5 [17], Qwen2.5-Coder [118],
837	CodeGemma [307], DeepSeek-Coder [50, 98], and CodeT5 [335, 337].
838	
839	  Model Scale (S1.3). The parameter count of an LLM typically serves as a proxy for its capacity
840	to learn complex patterns and encode domain knowledge. However, increasing scale imposes
841	proportional demands on computational resources for training and inference. Notably, there exists
842	no formal consensus regarding the exact parameter threshold that constitutes a "large" language
843	model. Despite this ambiguity, to analyze the trade-off between performance and resource efficiency,
844	we categorize the models used in the surveyed studies into four distinct groups:
845	
846	     • Tiny (S1.3.1): Models with fewer than 1 billion parameters (<1B). This category primarily
847	       includes pre-trained language models such as CodeBERT or UniXcoder. Due to their light-
848	       weight nature, they are highly efficient for fine-tuning and inference, making them suitable
849	       for resource-constrained environments.
850	     • Small (S1.3.2): Models with 1 to 8 billion parameters (1B–8B), such as Gemma-2B, Llama2-
851	       7B, or Llama3.1-8B. This scale represents a trade-off for many researchers; these models
852	       provide a significant improvement in generative capabilities over tiny models while remain-
853	       ing small enough to be deployed or fine-tuned on high-end consumer-grade hardware.
854	     • Medium (S1.3.3): Models between 8 and 70 billion parameters (8B–70B), including CodeLlama-
855	       34B, Mixtral 8x7B, and DeepSeek-R1-32B. These models typically outperform smaller coun-
856	       terparts in complex reasoning tasks but exceed the memory capacity of standard consumer
857	       hardware, necessitating enterprise-grade GPUs or multi-GPU setups.
858	     • Large (S1.3.4): Models exceeding 70 billion parameters (>70B), such as GPT-4, Llama3.1-
859	       405B, and DeepSeek-v3. These models achieve state-of-the-art performance on vulnerability
860	       detection benchmarks. However, due to their immense computational requirements, they
861	       are predominantly accessed via APIs or require extensive high-performance computing
862	       clusters for local deployment.
863	
864	  Figure 5 visualizes the relationship between model scale and adaptation techniques, e.g., fine-
865	tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and prompt engineering; highlighting that tiny and small
866	models are often fine-tuned in a full-parameter setting while large models are mainly prompted.
867	
868	=== [PDF page 16] ===
869	
870	16                                                                                          Kaniewski et al.
871	
872	
873	
874	
875	Fig. 5. Relationship between model scale and adaptation techniques across surveyed studies. Tiny and
876	small models are predominantly adapted via full-parameter fine-tuning, whereas medium and large models
877	increasingly utilize parameter-efficient fine-tuning and prompt engineering. Numbers in braces indicate the
878	absolute count of unique studies applying the respective adaptation techniques; a single study may apply
879	multiple adaptation techniques.
880	
881	
882	
883	4.3.2 Hybrid (S2). Hybrid architectures combine LLMs with other learning-based components to
884	leverage complementary strengths. Often, the LLM is used to produce embeddings that are subse-
885	quently processed by neural networks such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Convolutional
886	Neural Networks (CNNs), or Graph Neural Networks (GNNs).
887	   RNNs (S2.1) are neural architectures designed to handle sequential data by modeling temporal
888	and contextual dependencies between elements, e.g., syntactic, semantic, and control-flow relation-
889	ships [6]. Prominent RNN variants include Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs) and their
890	bidirectional forms (BiLSTMs), which are designed to handle long-range dependencies effectively. In
891	several studies, BERT embeddings are directly fed into (Bi-)LSTM networks [39, 163, 247, 356, 404].
892	   CNNs (S2.2) are neural architectures specialized in identifying local spatial patterns or features
893	within data through convolutional filters. Initially developed for image recognition tasks, CNNs
894	have been successfully adapted to textual and sequential data analysis by treating sequences as one-
895	dimensional spatial inputs. This capability allows CNNs to effectively capture localized syntactic
896	and semantic patterns in code sequences, making them useful for tasks such as vulnerability
897	detection [177]. Studies apply CNNs directly to code or graph embeddings [247, 379]. Others use
898	pre-trained embeddings within TextCNN architectures [108], or integrate CNNs with attention
899	mechanisms to enhance feature extraction [328, 353].
900	   GNNs (S2.3) are specialized neural architectures designed to operate directly on graph-structured
901	data, effectively modeling relationships between nodes and their structural dependencies. Given
902	structured representations of code, such as AST and CFG, several studies combine LLMs with
903	GNN-based architectures to take advantage of both sequential and structural representations of
904	code [177]. A common approach is to pass code embeddings, e.g., generated by CodeBERT or
905	GraphCodeBERT, into GNN-based classifiers [112, 152, 183, 221, 259, 299, 300, 313, 374, 390]. Other
906	studies use LLMs to feed graph embeddings [124, 125, 137, 254] or multiple modalities of a function,
907	including text, graph, and image representations [225] into Graph Convolution Networks (GCNs).
908	
909	=== [PDF page 17] ===
910	
911	A Systematic Literature Review on Detecting Software Vulnerabilities with Large Language Models           17
912	
913	
914	Yang et al. [362] use a GNN as a light-weight adapter layer and concatenate its learned embedding
915	with a fine-tuned LLM. Similarly, Gajjar et al. [85] use GCN and GAT to extract structural features,
916	subsequently fusing these graph embeddings with semantic embeddings derived from an LLM.
917	   Several hybrid architectures combine multiple neural components, integrating RNNs, CNNs,
918	and GNNs in sequence or parallel. For example, Chang et al. [32] process CodeBERT embeddings
919	using a two-layer GCN and a BiLSTM. Bahaa et al. [16] use a multi-layer approach composed of a
920	DistilBERT embedding layer followed by CNN and BiLSTM layers. Mei et al. [204] use CodeBERT
921	embeddings in three hybrid models, i.e., CLSTM, CBiLSTM (sequential structure), and CNN-BiLSTM
922	(parallel structure). JianJie and Le [138] present a multi-base classifier combining BERT-encoder,
923	GCN, CNN, and BiLSTM; the outputs are fused via stacking ensemble learning. Sun et al. [299]
924	propose a stacking ensemble strategy that integrates serialization-based and graph-based neural
925	networks to exploit complementary code semantics.
926	   Some studies [135, 205, 244, 247, 359] combine LLMs with Other (S2.4) learning-based com-
927	ponents that do not rely on RNNs, CNNs, or GNNs. For example, Melo et al. [205] evaluate the
928	effectiveness of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) when applied to representations from LLMs, which are
929	then classified using traditional machine learning models such as random forests. Jiang et al. [135]
930	pass embeddings to a Policy network for prediction. Peng et al. [244] use CodeBERT embeddings
931	as input to a Transformer-based classifier. Similarly, Xue et al. [359] perform feature fusion from
932	multiple pre-trained models and process the combined representation with a Transformer model.

934	4.4   Technique (T)
935	To use LLMs effectively for vulnerability detection, studies employ various techniques ranging
936	from simple prompting to complex system and training designs. We broadly categorize techniques
937	into three distinct strategies: (i) feature extraction, (ii) adaptation, and (iii) orchestration.
938	4.4.1 Feature Extraction. In the most simple approach, language models are used in their pre-
939	trained form without any additional training to extract features by generating input embeddings
940	(Feature Extraction (T1)) [61, 95, 110, 112, 124, 125, 128, 134, 135, 137, 156, 175, 198, 205, 221, 223,
941	225, 244, 247, 259, 297, 299, 300, 313, 328, 330, 353, 359, 374, 379, 388, 401]. These high-dimensional
942	vector representations capture the semantic and syntactic properties of the code and serve as input
943	for downstream classifiers.
944	4.4.2 Adaptation Technique (T2). Beyond using LLMs as static feature extractors, recent work
945	increasingly focuses on adapting LLMs to the vulnerability detection task through various state-of-
946	the-art techniques, which differ in how they modify the model’s parameters. The primary adaptation
947	techniques are pre-training, fine-tuning, and prompt engineering. Each technique reflects different
948	trade-offs between computational cost, model adaptation, and task-specific performance. In the
949	following, we discuss these adaptation techniques as observed in the surveyed studies.
950	    Prompt Engineering (T2.1). Prompt engineering refers to the design and structuring of input
951	prompts in a way that elicits desired behaviors or outputs without requiring any modifications to
952	the model’s weights. There are typically two types of prompts: a system prompt (providing general
953	context or behavioral instructions) and a user prompt (specifying the task and providing the code
954	to be analyzed). As LLMs remain sensitive to the phrasing, context, and formatting of prompts,
955	numerous prompting strategies have emerged to improve task alignment and performance.
956	    In Zero-Shot Prompting (T2.1.1), the model is expected to rely solely on its pre-trained knowl-
957	edge to perform vulnerability detection. The LLM is provided with the task description and input
958	(i.e., a potentially vulnerable code snippet under detection) [9, 15, 18, 31, 40, 41, 60, 65, 66, 68, 69, 72,
959	92, 102, 104, 119, 123, 146, 147, 153, 160, 170, 178, 185, 190, 193, 197, 199, 227, 231, 238, 239, 251, 261,

968	or No," targeted CWE-specific queries such as "Does the following code have a CWE-xxx vulner-
969	ability?", or openly phrased "Does this code have any vulnerabilities?" Studies often experiment

972	vulnerability detection system" [190]) to guide model behavior. Due to its simplicity, zero-shot
973	prompting is commonly used as a starting point and serves as a baseline for comparison with more
974	advanced prompting techniques.
975	   In-Context Learning (T2.1.2) refers to the prompt engineering technique of embedding addi-
976	tional contextual information (drawing upon the auxiliary information discussed, see Section 4.2)
977	into the model’s input to improve detection without parameter updates. Researchers frequently
978	provide vulnerability definitions, e.g., a candidate list of CWEs [18, 60, 83, 276, 293, 327, 355, 371] or
979	detailed vulnerability descriptions [24, 90, 202, 217, 284, 322]. Adopting a code-centric perspective,
980	studies also enrich prompts with execution context [3, 172, 210, 273, 301, 306, 381] or descriptions
981	of the code’s intended functionality [187, 190, 316, 364], supporting the vulnerability detection task.
982	Other approaches use a hybrid workflow by embedding prior detection results from static analysis
983	or similar tools, asking the LLM to verify or refine these findings [145, 219, 340, 365].
984	   Few-Shot Prompting (T2.1.3) [22], a specific in-context learning technique, provides the model
985	with one or multiple labeled input-output examples relevant to the task. By presenting these
986	examples in the prompt, the model is guided to infer the desired task behavior, enabling in-context
987	learning without modifying model weights. The examples used for few-shot prompting can be static,
988	i.e., manually selected and reused across prompts [37, 55, 59, 155, 173, 201, 227, 290, 319, 326, 368,
989	369], or vulnerability-specific, i.e., tailored examples targeting particular vulnerability types [72, 238,
990	322]. In another study, the examples are generated by the LLM itself [31]. Other common strategies
991	for example selection, as discussed by Steenhoek et al. [293], include using random vulnerable
992	and non-vulnerable examples from the training dataset [170, 217, 227, 238, 293, 349, 364, 394, 395],
993	constructing contrastive pairs where both a vulnerable code snippet and its corresponding fixed
994	version are provided within the same prompt [27, 232, 293, 364, 368], or selecting examples from
995	the training dataset based on similarity to the input code [109, 227, 286, 293, 321, 349, 395].
996	   Retrieval-Augmented Generation (T2.1.4) [158] extends the few-shot paradigm by dynamically
997	augmenting the prompt with relevant external information retrieved from a private knowledge base.
998	Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems use a retriever component to identify and fetch
999	contextually similar entries based on embedding similarity or other relevance metrics, e.g., BM25.
1000	The LLM then works with the provided knowledge to generate the output. A key advantage of RAG
1001	over few-shot prompting is its ability to dynamically incorporate domain-specific and up-to-date
1002	knowledge, making it especially useful for integrating evolving vulnerability knowledge. In the
1003	context of vulnerability detection, RAG-based approaches use a wide range of retrieval content.
1004	Some studies retrieve the most similar code snippets or code dependencies along with known
1005	vulnerability information [139, 187, 190, 193, 238, 270, 278, 293, 320, 321, 345, 365, 382, 397, 399].
1006	Others rely on abstract code functionality and vulnerability descriptions to better capture the
1007	vulnerability semantics and context of the input code [63, 173, 284, 301]. Additionally, vulnerability
1008	reports and CWE descriptions are retrieved to guide the model’s reasoning using structured
1009	vulnerability information [24, 145, 153, 202, 243, 273].
1010	   Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting (T2.1.5) [342] aims at enhancing the reasoning capabilities
1011	of LLMs by encouraging intermediate reasoning steps before arriving at a final prediction. Reasoning
1012	behavior is typically triggered by simple cues such as "Let’s think step by step" [15, 55, 59, 119, 227,
1013	243, 270, 278, 293, 322, 326, 347, 368, 394, 403], requests for explanation [37, 146, 160, 364], or specific

1031	   Training (T2.2). The adaptation of LLMs to software vulnerability detection tasks often follows the
1032	established pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm: models are trained from scratch (Pre-Training
1033	(T2.2.1)) using large code corpora to capture programming-specific syntax and semantics [2, 8,
1034	23, 56, 57, 108, 117, 128, 136, 162, 189, 336, 358, 372] and further fine-tuned for domain-specific
1035	applications. Fine-Tuning (T2.2.2) is the most widely adopted technique. Studies adopt a range of
1036	fine-tuning strategies that vary in their degree of parameter update and architectural design.
1037	   Full-Parameter Fine-Tuning (T2.2.2.1) refers to tuning all parameters of a pre-trained language
1038	model for the downstream task of vulnerability detection. Models are either fine-tuned by replacing
1039	the last output layer [94] with a classification head (e.g., a multi-layer perceptron), which return the
1040	probability of vulnerability; or fine-tuned as a generative model where the response is matched to
1041	keywords such as “vulnerable” or “non vulnerable”. Full-parameter fine-tuning is widely adopted in
1042	the surveyed studies [2, 5, 8, 12–14, 16, 23, 31, 35, 36, 39, 41, 44, 47, 51, 55–57, 64, 67, 76, 79, 81, 82, 85,
1043	87, 94, 102, 103, 105, 106, 108, 117, 120, 130, 136, 138, 140–142, 149, 152, 154, 155, 163, 167, 170, 171,
1044	176, 180, 182–184, 189, 194, 196, 199, 200, 203, 204, 216, 220, 222, 224, 228, 235, 236, 241, 249, 251,
1045	252, 254, 258, 262, 263, 268, 269, 280, 281, 283, 284, 288, 289, 292, 294–296, 298, 303, 305, 311, 312,
1046	316, 336, 338, 339, 344–347, 354, 356, 358, 363, 369, 375, 377, 378, 386, 389–391, 394, 398, 401, 404],
1047	particularly with tiny models, see Figure 5. While full-parameter fine-tuning is computationally
1048	intensive and less reusable across tasks, it allows the model to specialize in vulnerability detection
1049	by adapting all internal representations.
1050	   A specific variant of fine-tuning is Instruction-Tuning (T2.2.2.1.1), where a language model
1051	is fine-tuned on labeled input-output pairs annotated with natural language instructions [19, 62,
1052	126, 133, 160, 201, 286, 293, 314, 350, 376, 382, 383], e.g., "Instruction: Detect whether the following
1053	code contains vulnerabilities" [133]. This method allows the model to better follow human-written
1054	prompts by learning general patterns for task completion. In [350], Widyasari et al. use GPT-4o for
1055	generating the instructions. Instruction-tuning has shown promise in enhancing performance on
1056	unseen instructions and is often combined with parameter-efficient (rather than full) fine-tuning
1057	techniques to reduce training cost [62, 133, 160, 201, 286, 314, 376, 382, 383].
1058	
1059	   Key drawbacks of full-parameter fine-tuning are its high computational cost and the potential
1060	harm to the model’s generalization ability. To address these drawbacks, several studies adopt
1061	Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) (T2.2.2.2) techniques, which adapt only a small subset of
1062	model parameters or learn external modules for new tasks while keeping most of the pre-trained
1063	parameters frozen. To categorize the PEFT methods, we adopt the taxonomy by Han et al. [107],
1064	covering (i) selective, (ii) additive, and (iii) reparameterized PEFT techniques.
1065	   In Selective PEFT (T2.2.2.2.1), only a small subset of model parameters is selected for fine-tuning,
1066	while keeping the other parameters frozen. In the surveyed studies, the final [381] or upper model
1067	layer(s) [34] were fine-tuned to generate contextual embeddings.

1074	   Additive PEFT (T2.2.2.2.2) techniques introduce a small number of trainable parameters that are
1075	strategically positioned within the model architecture. During fine-tuning, only the weights of
1076	these additional modules or parameters are updated, reducing storage, memory, and computational
1077	resource requirements. Prominent additive PEFT techniques are adapter-tuning and prompt-tuning.
1078	   Adapter-Tuning (T2.2.2.2.2.1) inserts small trainable neural modules, i.e., adapters, into a frozen
1079	pre-trained model. During fine-tuning, only the adapter parameters are updated, while the model’s
1080	parameters remain unchanged [4, 162]. Rather than employing default configurations that use the
1081	same adapter settings across all layers, Akli et al. [4] present AutoAdapt to automatically discover
1082	task-specific, layer-wide adapter configurations, allowing each layer to adopt distinct parameters.
1083	   Prompt-Tuning (T2.2.2.2.2.2) involves learning prompts to improve model performance on a
1084	downstream task. Two main prompt forms are distinguished: hard prompts, which are manually
1085	crafted sequences of tokens appended to the input, and soft prompts, which are learned continuous
1086	embeddings that serve as virtual tokens prepended to the input. Prompt-tuning keeps the model
1087	weights frozen while tuning only the parameters of the soft prompts [32, 38, 73, 194, 260]. Various
1088	adaptations of prompt-tuning have been investigated. Ren et al. [260] integrate prompt-tuning
1089	with a reinforcement learning framework. Feng et al. [73] explore graph-enhanced prompt-tuning,
1090	which incorporates structural code information by embedding graph features into soft prompts.
1091	   Apart from the methods mentioned above, another additive approach has been used that strate-
1092	gically trains additional parameters during the fine-tuning process (Additive-Other (T2.2.2.2.2.3)):
1093	Li et al. [161] introduce a vulnerability steering vector that represents the concept of vulnerability
1094	in the representation space. The vector is injected into the activation values of the corresponding
1095	layer, guiding the model’s behavior without modifying all its parameters.
1096	   Reparameterized PEFT (T2.2.2.2.3) techniques transform a model’s architecture by modifying how
1097	its parameters are represented and trained. This typically involves replacing large components of the
1098	model with smaller, low-rank versions during training, reducing the number of parameters that need
1099	to be updated. At inference time, the model can be converted to its original parameterization [107].
1100	   The most widely adopted reparameterization technique in the surveyed studies is categorized
1101	as Low-Rank Decomposition (T2.2.2.2.3.1): LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) [115]. LoRA injects
1102	trainable low-rank decomposition matrices into the attention layers of a frozen language model,
1103	enabling task-specific adaptation with significantly fewer parameters [7, 12, 25, 38, 43, 62, 86, 91,
1104	102, 128, 133, 157, 160, 170, 182, 197, 201, 250, 280, 286, 329, 347, 348, 376, 383, 394, 400].
1105	   LoRA Derivatives (T2.2.2.2.3.2) have also been explored to improve efficiency and adaptability.
1106	Tian et al. [314] use PiSSA (Principal Singular Values and Singular Vectors Adaptation) [206],
1107	which shares the same architecture as LoRA but adopts a different initialization method. Ibanez-
1108	Lissen et al. [120] use GaLore (Gradient Low-Rank Projection) [385], a memory-efficient training
1109	strategy that allows full-parameter training while requiring less memory than common low-rank
1110	approaches. Another efficient PEFT design is QLoRA (Quantized LoRA) [52], which applies LoRA
1111	to a quantized version of the language model to further reduce memory consumption. QLoRA has
1112	been used in multiple surveyed studies to efficiently fine-tune large models for code vulnerability
1113	tasks [238, 298, 302, 343, 362, 382].

1115	  Learning Paradigms (T2.3). Beyond standard supervised fine-tuning, several advanced learning
1116	paradigms have been employed to enhance the performance and generalization capabilities of
1117	vulnerability detection models, e.g., contrastive learning, causal learning, multi-task learning,
1118	knowledge distillation, continual learning, and reinforcement learning.
1119	  Contrastive Learning (T2.3.1) aims to learn more discriminative representations by encouraging
1120	the model to pull semantically similar instances closer and push dissimilar ones apart in the
1121	representation space, thereby improving the model’s ability to distinguish between structurally

1129	contrastive learning techniques to the vulnerability detection domain [55, 61, 85, 130, 134, 162,
1130	228, 329, 336, 354]. Notably, Du et al. [61] propose mutual nearest neighbor contrastive learning to
1131	align the source and target domains. Ding et al. [55] introduce class-aware contrastive learning,
1132	which minimizes similarity only between samples with different class labels to improve type-
1133	specific discrimination. Ji et al. [130] present a hierarchical contrastive learning framework to bring

1135	contrastive losses to promote geometric spread and improved inter-class separation.
1136	   Causal Learning (T2.3.2) guides models to focus on genuine cause-and-effect relationships
1137	rather than relying on spurious correlations in the code, e.g., variable or API names that are not
1138	actual causes of vulnerabilities. Rahman et al. [258] identify such spurious features via semantic-
1139	preserving perturbations (e.g., variable renaming or dead-code injection) and then systematically
1140	remove their influence using causal inference techniques. Specifically, they simulate interventions,
1141	i.e., asking how the model would behave if certain spurious features were actively changed, and
1142	block non-causal paths by conditioning on known spurious features. This strategy allows the model
1143	to rely on causally relevant features and, thereby, improve robustness and generalization to unseen
1144	or perturbed code scenarios, such as different projects or naming conventions.
1145	   Multi-Task Learning (T2.3.3) has emerged as an effective paradigm for improving general-
1146	ization by jointly training on related tasks, thereby reducing overfitting and enhancing model
1147	robustness across a range of tasks. Several studies adopt multi-task learning to enhance vulner-
1148	ability analysis: Fu et al. [82] fine-tune under the multi-task setting for predicting CWE-ID and
1149	CWE-type, while Chen et al. [34] combine CWE-ID classification with line-level vulnerability de-
1150	tection. Curto et al. [44] perform binary vulnerability detection alongside multi-class vulnerability
1151	categorization. Similarly, Steenhoek et al. [295] fine-tune for simultaneous binary classification,
1152	multi-class vulnerability type prediction, and localization. Islam et al. [125] combine vulnerability
1153	classification with description. Du et al. [62] apply multi-task instruction-tuning for vulnerability
1154	detection, localization, and interpretation of root causes; while Yang et al. [362] focus on multi-task
1155	fine-tuning for vulnerability detection, explanation, and repair. Russo et al. [268] leverage shared
1156	information between self-admitted technical debt (SATD) and vulnerabilities to jointly detect both
1157	issues, Alqarni and Azim [7] combine the analysis of code, system calls, and bitstreams, and Ding
1158	et al. [56] use multi-task pre-training to jointly learn static and dynamic code properties.
1159	   Knowledge Distillation (T2.3.4) is a model compression strategy in which a smaller model, i.e.,
1160	the student, is trained to replicate the behavior of a larger model, i.e., the teacher. By learning from
1161	the teacher’s output distributions, the student achieves comparable performance while significantly
1162	reducing computational cost, making it suitable for resource-constrained settings. Some studies
1163	directly adopt pre-trained distilled models such as DistilBERT for vulnerability detection [47,
1164	176, 182], while other studies apply knowledge distillation explicitly, using teacher and student
1165	LLMs [184, 235, 241, 281, 343, 348], or a setup with CNN and GNN models to distill knowledge
1166	into or from a LLM backbone [79, 106, 183, 224]. A more advanced approach is presented by Fu
1167	et al. [79], who introduce a hierarchical knowledge distillation framework. The CWE label space
1168	is split into multiple sub-distributions based on semantic similarity, and individual CNN teacher
1169	models are trained on each subset. A student language model then learns to generalize across the
1170	teacher outputs, improving its ability to handle multi-class vulnerability detection tasks. Han et
1171	al. [106] follow this approach with an enhanced memory mechanism. Panichella [241] combines
1172	metamorphic testing with many-objective optimization for distillation of LLMs for code, measuring
1173	model robustness across semantically equivalent code variants.

1206	using only positively (vulnerable) labeled and unlabeled data [152, 346]. Forms of active learning
1207	aim to reduce labeling costs by strategically selecting the most informative samples for annota-

1210	learning, the most suitable data is selected for each training epoch, from easy to hard learning
1211	samples [39]. Adversarial training enhances model robustness by introducing crafted perturbed
1212	code examples during training, improving robustness to noise and attacks [34, 62, 184, 372, 389].

1215	4.4.3 Orchestration Technique (T3). While adaptation techniques focus on optimizing the model’s
1216	internal parameters or input context, orchestration techniques focus on the design of the inference
1217	process. Rather than relying on a simple input-model-output pipeline, orchestration techniques
1218	embed the LLM into advanced system designs that utilize multiple generation steps, iterative
1219	refinement, or collaborative workflows. We categorize orchestration techniques into Multi-Step,
1220	Verification, Agentic, Ensemble, and Controller-based systems.
1221	   Some studies engage the model in a Multi-Step (T3.1) analysis, rather than issuing a single
1222	prompt for vulnerability detection [55, 68, 119, 139, 187, 190, 210, 245, 320, 322, 326, 364, 371]. A
1223	common strategy within this approach is to decouple comprehension from detection, prompt-
1224	ing the model to first analyze the code’s functionality or intent before querying for vulnerabili-
1225	ties [68, 119, 139, 187, 190, 245, 326, 364]. Beyond functional analysis, Yu et al. [371] task the model
1226	to first generate supplementary code files based on commit messages, subsequently using this
1227	supplementary context for the final detection. Mhatre et al. [210] follow a debugging style, first
1228	identifying code issues, followed by a deeper, targeted analysis of specific issues. Tsai et al. [320]
1229	propose a sequential approach that dynamically selects the optimal strategy, choosing between

1238	   To mitigate hallucinations and improve precision, studies increasingly adopt Verification (T3.2)
1239	mechanisms where models are prompted to review and improve generated outputs. Verification
1240	extends the standard prompt-response interaction by re-prompting the model to evaluate, validate,
1241	or refine a prediction. In single-model setups, the model is typically prompted to assess its prior
1242	response by verifying the correctness of its output [355] or by recursively critiquing and improv-
1243	ing [62, 273, 306]. In multi-model settings, verification is implemented as an interactive process
1244	between models (collaborative refinement), possibly under different roles. For example, using the
1245	output of one model to prompt another model with corrective cues such as "An expert has found...
1246	please recheck it" [9, 24, 66, 321, 339, 349].
1247	   Agentic (T3.3) systems embed LLMs into autonomous, decision-making loops, following a higher-
1248	level behavioral pattern involving multi-step planning, tool use, and self-directed reasoning. Agents
1249	may operate individually or as part of multi-agent systems [3, 24, 66, 168, 320, 321, 340, 350, 368],
1250	where agents specialize in subtasks or roles, interact with tools, and collaboratively refine outputs.
1251	For example, Yildiz et al. [368] employ Reasoning and Acting (ReAct) agents [366], which follow
1252	a thought-action-observation cycle, for vulnerability detection in code repositories. Widyasari
1253	et al. [350] present a courtroom-inspired multi-agent framework with four role-specific agents:
1254	security researcher, code author, moderator, and review board. The agents collaborate to assess
1255	code vulnerabilities through iterative analysis, argumentation, summarization, and a final verdict
1256	based on collective reasoning. Ahmed et al. [3] propose a multi-agent pipeline consisting of a
1257	normalization, planning, context, detection, and validation agent. Sayagh and Ghafari [273] use
1258	multiple agentic teams, with a lister searching for potential CWEs in the input code, a reviewer
1259	requesting missing CWEs, further agents identifying external code context, and a final agent
1260	deciding on each CWE based on gathered context.
1261	   Ensemble (T3.4) approaches combine the representations or predictions of diverse models to
1262	mitigate individual model limitations and biases. To leverage complementary feature representa-
1263	tions, e.g., semantic, contextual, and syntactic features, studies fuse representations from different
1264	pre-trained models [64, 138, 198, 262, 283, 299, 354, 356]. For example, Ridoy et al. [262] employ an
1265	ensemble stacking approach to synthesize the semantic understanding of CodeBERT, the structural
1266	representations of GraphCodeBERT, and the cross-modal capabilities of UniXcoder. Distinct from
1267	standard feature fusion, Tian et al. [312] introduce a parameter fusion method that merges inde-
1268	pendent classification heads trained on distinct vulnerability datasets, allowing the model to adapt
1269	to new vulnerability types. Ensemble approaches further include decision-level aggregation via
1270	voting mechanisms to combine predictions from multiple LLMs [349, 382] or ensembles of LLMs
1271	and other tools [382, 394].
1272	   Moving beyond static inference pipelines, some studies use LLMs in a Controller (T3.5) or
1273	collaboration setting. A central model or routing mechanism analyzes the input code and coordinates
1274	downstream resources, selecting, e.g., the most appropriate expert models or prompts. Yang et
1275	al. [363] and Wu and Xiao [354] implement a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework where a
1276	router dynamically assigns input code to the most appropriate vulnerability experts. Similarly,
1277	Wang et al. [340] employ a meta-agent to route code to specialized analyzers. Peng et al. [245]
1278	introduce a Mixture-of-Prompts architecture that activates specific prompt experts (dynamic
1279	prompt pipelines) based on code features of the code under detection. Li et al. [160] simulate team
1280	collaboration involving a leader and various expert models specialized on syntactic features; the
1281	leader orchestrates the process and derives the final detection from the experts’ analyses. Farr et
1282	al. [72] extend the routing logic to human collaborators. They flag code as automatic quarantine,

1292	5    Vulnerability Datasets
1293	In this SLR, we set an emphasis on investigating the datasets used in the adaptation and evaluation of
1294	LLM-based vulnerability detection approaches. Datasets play a central role: Their quality, structure,
1295	and coverage of diverse vulnerability types directly affect model performance and generalization.
1296	Further, the choice of dataset does not merely benchmark performance. A critical challenge in this
1297	domain is data leakage, where data samples overlap with the corpora used to pre-train the model,
1298	potentially leading to inflated performance.
1299	   Furthermore, the use of datasets has evolved beyond standard training. With the rise of advanced
1300	prompting techniques, datasets now serve as a dynamic input context, providing exemplars for in-
1301	context prompting or knowledge retrieval. This shift also changes which parts of the data are used.
1302	While deep learning-based models often relied solely on code syntax, LLMs actively leverage the
1303	natural language components of datasets, such as commit messages, vulnerability descriptions, and
1304	code comments, to support high-level explanation and reasoning tasks. Therefore, systematically
1305	comparing datasets is essential to understand their suitability for LLM-based detection, assess their
1306	limitations, and ensure meaningful evaluations.
1307	   To systematically analyze the datasets used in the surveyed studies, we extend the presented
1308	taxonomy to cover datasets. We outline the taxonomy based on the datasets used most commonly
1309	for training or evaluation in the surveyed studies, discussing type, granularity, source, and labeling.
1310	Further, we investigate the CWE coverage and diversity of selected datasets, discussing limitations
1311	such as long-tail distributions and a lack of representative vulnerability coverage. Finally, we discuss
1312	trends in dataset usage, emphasizing the comparability of evaluations across different use cases.
1313
