1346	5.1.1 Dataset Type. We distinguish three dataset types: (i) synthetic, (ii) real-world, and (iii) mixed.
1347	   Synthetic datasets are artificially generated, often by injecting predefined vulnerability patterns
1348	into source code. The synthetic datasets Juliet C/C++ [208] and Juliet Java [209] (subsets of the
1349	Software Assurance Reference Dataset (SARD) [207]) provide comprehensive sets of test cases and
1350	entire test suites. These test suites are widely used to benchmark both traditional static analysis
1351	tools and deep learning-based vulnerability detectors. A key strength of synthetic datasets lies in
1352	their reliable labels, as they inject known vulnerable patterns into code, thereby ensuring clear
1353	ground truth annotations. However, this injection-based approach often results in limited code
1354	diversity and reduced realism, as the code samples tend to be simple and may not reflect the
1355	complexity of real-world source code. Further, the manual effort required to represent a diverse set
1356	of vulnerabilities can be labor-intensive.
1357	   Real-World datasets are sourced from open-source software projects, e.g., Devign [396], or
1358	curated vulnerability databases, e.g., Big-Vul [71] and MegaVul [226]. These datasets are more
1359	suited for a realistic evaluation, capturing the challenges posed by detecting software vulnerabilities
1360	in real-world projects. However, due to the efforts required for crawling and parsing software
1361	projects, real-world datasets often suffer from label noise.
1362	   Mixed datasets combine real-world code with synthetic data, leveraging augmentation to enrich
1363	or balance the dataset. For example, the SARD [207] dataset contains a mix of production, synthetic,
1364	and academic vulnerable samples. VulDeePecker [174] combines samples from SARD and the
1365	National Vulnerability Database (NVD) [234]. Draper [267] combines synthetic functions from
1366	the Juliet test suite with open-source code from software packages and public repositories. Mixed
1367	datasets offer a practical trade-off between realism and control, making them particularly valuable
1368	for covering underrepresented or rare vulnerability types.
1369	
1370	5.1.2 Dataset Granularity. Vulnerabilities can occur at various structural levels within the software,
1371	from single lines to entire files. Dataset granularity refers to the level at which code is labeled or
1372	segmented within the dataset. Following Shereen et al. [279], we differentiate coarse, medium, and
1373	fine-grained levels.
1374	   Coarse-grained datasets operate at the Project, Commit, or File level. ReposVul [332] focuses
1375	on extracting dependencies on multiple granularity levels, including repository-level and file-level.
1376	Similarly, CrossVul [230] labels samples at the file level, thereby aligning closely with practical use
1377	cases in vulnerability detection. While this level of granularity offers realistic scenarios for analysis,
1378	it also introduces a high risk of noise due to the large code context surrounding the vulnerability.
1379	   Medium-grained datasets segment code at the Program, Slice or Function level. The largest
1380	share of commonly used vulnerability datasets is labeled at the function level [21, 30, 35, 54, 63, 71,
1381	171, 207, 226, 267, 392, 396], cf. Table 4. The VulDeePecker dataset, also known as the Code Gadget
1382	Database (CGD), represents program slices as code gadgets composed of a number of program
1383	statements that are semantically related to each other through data or control dependencies. While
1384	this granularity supports a more focused analysis, it may miss critical contextual information when
1385	vulnerabilities span multiple functions or require interprocedural analysis.
1386	   Fine-grained datasets label vulnerabilities at the Line level, enabling precise vulnerability lo-
1387	calization. Big-Vul, D2A [392], FormAI, and ReposVul provide annotations at the line-level. Such
1388	a narrow scope, however, omits the broader context required to detect certain vulnerabilities,
1389	especially those involving complex data flows or control dependencies.

1423	5.1.3 Dataset Source. To categorize the source of the dataset, we adapt the four categories defined
1424	by Hou et al. [114], i.e., (i) open-source, (ii) collected, (iii) constructed, and (iv) closed-source.
1425	   Open-Source datasets are derived from public data collections accessible through open-source
1426	platforms or repositories, e.g., Github repositories. Examples for open-source datasets are SARD,
1427	Devign, D2A, and CleanVul [171]. Their accessibility ensures transparency and reproducibility,
1428	making them widely used in academic research. However, datasets sourced directly from GitHub
1429	repositories often lack reliable ground-truth labels and are sensitive to repository selection and
1430	curation quality, i.e., the specific projects chosen and how samples are filtered, labeled, and balanced,
1431	leading to biased, noisy, or unrepresentative data.
1432	   Collected datasets are those scraped, mined, and extracted by researchers from various sources
1433	such as security trackers or related databases (e.g., NVD [234], CVE [46], or CWE database [213]).
1434	MegaVul, for example, is collected by crawling the CVE database along with CVE-related open-
1435	source projects hosted across Git-based platforms. While authoritative vulnerability records provide
1436	structured metadata and standardized vulnerability classifications, the mapping of records to source
1437	code can be non-trivial and may miss undocumented or undisclosed vulnerabilities.
1438	   Constructed datasets are created by modifying or augmenting one or multiple other (collected)
1439	datasets, either manually or using semi-automatic methods, to better align with domain-specific
1440	objectives, e.g., focusing on specific CWEs or programming languages. Constructed datasets include
1441	the mixed datasets VulDeePecker and Draper. Further, SecurityEval [287] is constructed from
1442	sources such as GitHub’s CodeQL documentation, the CWE database, Sonar static analyzer rules,
1443	and prior Copilot-based studies. Additional samples were crafted by the authors. SVEN [111] refines
1444	and validates samples from Big-Vul, CrossVul, and VUDENC [341], focusing on nine common
1445	CWE types. The PrimeVul dataset [54] merges and de-duplicates data from Big-Vul, CrossVul,
1446	CVEfixes [21], and DiverseVul [35].
1447	   Closed-Source datasets are obtained from commercial or industrial entities. Closed-sourced
1448	datasets are absent from the listed commonly used datasets. Notably, only few surveyed stud-
1449	ies [57, 216, 245, 359] use an industrial, closed-sourced dataset. Although such datasets offer

1460	5.1.4 Dataset Labeling. Accurate labeling is essential for constructing high-quality vulnerability
1461	datasets and reliable evaluations. To categorize the labeling of datasets, we adopt the four main
1462	label origin categories by Croft et al. [42]: (i) security vendor-provided, (ii) developer-provided,
1463	(iii) tool-created, and (iv) synthetically created.
1464	    Security Vendor-provided labels are derived from curated vulnerability databases maintained
1465	by security vendors, i.e., organizations that collect and standardize information on disclosed
1466	vulnerabilities from various advisories. An example database is the NVD. Many entries include
1467	links to corresponding patches on security trackers or GitHub sites, enabling the mapping of
1468	vulnerabilities to real-world source code. For example, the Big-Vul dataset was collected by crawling
1469	the public CVE database and linking the CVE entries to related source code changes in GitHub
1470	projects. This labeling strategy is reliable and consistent with real-world vulnerability disclosures.
1471	However, it is limited to publicly disclosed cases and includes historical data with labels that may
1472	not align with up-to-date vulnerability mappings [332].
1473	    Developer-provided labels are extracted directly from a project’s development history or issue
1474	tracker systems on platforms such as GitHub. A commonly used strategy involves vulnerability
1475	fixing commits (VFCs), identifying vulnerable code before a fix and secure code after a fix. VFCs
1476	are often identified via project references by the NVD or keyword search. The Devign dataset
1477	(also referred to as FFmpeg and QEMU) consists of vulnerable functions extracted from VFCs
1478	identified via keyword-based filtering and manually labeled by security researchers. Devign is
1479	also part of the CodeXGLUE benchmark [195]. Contrary to manually labeling VFCs, relying solely
1480	on VFCs often results in noisy labels due to the simplifying assumption that all pre-commit code
1481	is vulnerable and all post-commit code is secure [42]. In practice, VFCs may contain unrelated
1482	changes such as refactoring or test updates, and fixes are sometimes distributed across multiple
1483	commits. Further, labeling based solely on modified lines may overlook vulnerable context and
1484	cross-line dependencies. To address these challenges, newer datasets propose refined VFC labeling
1485	strategies. The PrimeVul dataset [54] uses two labeling strategies: PRIMEVUL-ONEFUNC, which
1486	marks a function as vulnerable only if it is the only function modified by a VFC, and PRIMEVUL-
1487	NVDCHECK, which cross-references CVE descriptions with modified functions. CleanVul addresses
1488	the label noise using an LLM, which assigns a confidence score from 0 (no vulnerability detected)
1489	to 4 (very high likelihood of vulnerability) to identify vulnerability-fixing changes and filter out
1490	unrelated modifications such as test updates or refactorings.
1491	    Tool-created labels are automatically generated using, e.g., static analyzers or formal verification
1492	tools. For instance, in the Draper dataset, labels are generated using static analyzers and then
1493	manually mapped to binary vulnerability labels and CWEs by a team of security experts. Similarly,
1494	the D2A dataset applies differential analysis to VFC version pairs from several open-source projects
1495	using static analysis tools, identifying disappearing bugs likely to present true vulnerabilities.
1496	Notably, the FormAI dataset [315] consists of compilable and self-contained C programs generated
1497	using GPT-3.5-Turbo, incorporating varying levels of complexity to simulate a broad spectrum of
1498	coding patterns. Labels are derived using formal verification. ReposVul jointly employs LLMs for
1499	evaluating the relevance between code changes and vulnerability fixes and static analysis tools for
1500	checking the vulnerabilities in the changes. While tools enable large-scale dataset creation, they are
1501	often criticized for generating a high volume of false positives. Static analysis tools, in particular,
1502	produce numerous warnings, many of which originate from low-confidence detections [42]. Formal
1503	verification offers higher detection reliability but at higher computational costs.

1542	ating controlled artificial samples, e.g., as used by the synthetic Juliet test suites. This method is

1544	oversimplify the complexity of real-world vulnerabilities.
1545	5.1.5 Dataset Programming Language. Commonly used vulnerability datasets are heavily biased
1546	towards C/C++, as shown in Table 5. While this bias reflects the prevalence of these languages in
1547	technological infrastructure, it creates a significant imbalance, as vulnerability patterns are intrinsi-
1548	cally linked to the programming language. Qian et al. [253] highlight that unmanaged languages
1549	such as C/C++ are prone to memory safety violations (e.g., buffer overflows), whereas managed
1550	languages such as JavaScript or Python frequently suffer from logic bugs. In a comparative analysis
1551	of interpreted languages (Java, JavaScript, Python, and Ruby), Ruohonen [266] observes that while
1552	certain weaknesses such as cross-site scripting and input validation errors are ubiquitous across
1553	all ecosystems, language-specific trends emerge. For instance, cryptographic issues were found to
1554	be prevalent in JavaScript but significantly less common in Java or Python [266]. Consequently,
1555	the predominance of C/C++ risks over-optimizing models for memory safety violations while
1556	potentially neglecting the distinct vulnerability landscapes of modern web languages.
1557	   Fewer datasets cover multiple programming languages, i.e., SARD, CVEfixes, CrossVul, and
1558	CleanVul; however, they are not represented in the same share. Recent studies have begun con-
1559	structing datasets for less covered languages, e.g., Python [239] and Rust [197], contributing to
1560	broader language diversity in vulnerability research.
1561	5.1.6 Dataset Size and Share of Vulnerable Samples. The size of a dataset is strongly influenced
1562	by the dataset source and its labeling method. Smaller datasets typically involve manual curation,
1563	enabling high label quality but limited scalability. SecurityEval, for example, focuses on evaluating

1577	   The dataset type and the labeling method used in dataset construction influence both the quality
1578	and realism, cf. Figure 7. Synthetic datasets, such as Juliet or FormAI, offer high label accuracy due
1579	to controlled injection of known vulnerability patterns but often lack the structural complexity and
1580	semantic diversity found in real-world code. In contrast, datasets derived from real-world sources
1581	provide greater realism, better reflecting practical vulnerability scenarios. However, they often
1582	suffer from label noise due to assumptions inherent in VFC-based labeling. These datasets also vary
1583	in the proportion of vulnerable samples. Highly imbalanced datasets, i.e., where vulnerabilities
1584	are underrepresented, reflect the natural rarity of vulnerabilities in real code. While realistic, such
1585	an imbalance poses challenges for training models, which may become biased towards predicting
1586	the majority class. To mitigate this challenge, preprocessing techniques are often required, e.g.,
1587	resampling: oversampling the minority (vulnerable) class or undersampling the majority (non-
1588	vulnerable) class to achieve a more balanced class distribution. Figure 7 visualizes this trade-off
1589	between labeling accuracy and realism, providing a practical framework for selecting datasets for
1590	different research objectives.
1591	5.1.7 Dataset Multi-Class Labeling. Vulnerability detection is often framed as a binary classification
1592	task, i.e., distinguishing between vulnerable and non-vulnerable code. For example, the ReVeal
1593	dataset provides security-related patches collected from bug tracking systems, offering paired
1594	vulnerable and fixed code samples labeled in binary form.
1595	   Many datasets go beyond binary classification by providing labels for specific vulnerability types,
1596	enabling multi-class and multi-label classification. CVEfixes is a comprehensive and automatically
1597	curated dataset collected from CVE entries in the NVD. It identifies linked open-source projects
1598	and extracts function-level vulnerable and fixed code samples from VFCs. The latest release at the
1599	time of writing (v1.0.8) includes all CVEs published up to July 23, 2024, covering 272 distinct CWEs.

1635	   A common limitation across vulnerability datasets is the lack of coverage of recently disclosed
1636	vulnerabilities. Static datasets may quickly become outdated, reducing their relevance for real-time
1637	or forward-looking research. In addition, this temporal lag introduces a critical validity threat for
1638	LLMs in the form of data leakage. Since widely used static datasets are likely contained within the
1639	pre-training corpora of LLMs and new models are continuously emerging, high performance on
1640	these benchmarks may indicate memorization rather than genuine generalization. This challenge
1641	highlights the need for continuously maintained and extensible datasets, e.g., CVEfixes, which is
1642	supported by an automated pipeline, to ensure evaluation against novel, unseen vulnerabilities.
1643	   Datasets such as Big-Vul, CrossVul, CVEfixes, and ReposVul further offer rich metadata, in-
1644	cluding CWE descriptions and severity scores. Such metadata supports diverse generative tasks,
1645	for example, root-cause reasoning and context-aware vulnerability analysis, broadening their use
1646	beyond classification.
1647	
1648	5.2   CWE Coverage and Diversity
1649	To assess the real-world applicability and limitations of LLM-based vulnerability detection ap-
1650	proaches, it is crucial to use datasets that capture a diverse range of vulnerability types. Such
1651	diversity enables more realistic evaluations, as it reflects the variety and complexity of vulnerabili-
1652	ties encountered in practical software development. As shown in Table 5, the number and variety of
1653	vulnerability types (i.e., number of CWE classes) represented vary considerably across the selected
1654	datasets. Some datasets focus narrowly on specific vulnerability types and CWE classes, while
1655	others aim for broader CWE diversity. To assess the diversity and composition of CWEs, we analyze
1656	selected real-world and mixed datasets providing multi-class labels (cf. Table 4) in more depth,
1657	focusing on their CWE coverage and distribution. Specifically, we analyze VulDeePecker, Draper,
1658	Big-Vul, CVEfixes, CrossVul, SecurityEval, DiverseVul, SVEN, ReposVul, PrimeVul, PairVul, and
1659	MegaVul. D2A and FormAI are excluded from this analysis. D2A is not considered, as it provides
1660	only static analyzer outputs without CWE annotations. Similarly, FormAI, while performing manual
1661	CWE mapping, does not include these mappings as part of the dataset but only error types provided
1662	by the formal verification tool.
1663	   As discussed in prior works [51, 133, 226], real-world vulnerability datasets exhibit a characteristic
1664	long-tail distribution: A small number of CWE types are heavily represented, while the majority of
1665	CWE types appear only rarely, often with just one or two examples. This characteristic is visualized
1666	in Figure 8, which shows the count of CWEs for the 15 most and least represented CWE classes for
1667	selected datasets. For example, while CVEfixes covers 272 distinct CWE types, the majority are
1668	sparsely represented. A similar pattern is observed for DiverseVul, which covers 150 CWEs. Such
1669	skewed distributions lead to biased learning, where models disproportionately focus on a small
1670	subset of vulnerability types. MegaVul and SecurityEval represent efforts to encourage a more
1671	balanced representation. SecurityEval, in particular, provides one to six manually curated examples
1672	for 69 CWEs. These efforts represent a step towards reducing long-tail effects and developing more
1673	generalizable vulnerability detection models.
1674	   For a more structured comparison of the CWE distributions across the datasets, we adopt the
1675	CWE-1000 Research View [211]. This view provides a hierarchical grouping of CWEs intended
1676	for research and analysis. It groups CWEs into broad research concepts to help identify inter-
1677	dependencies, shared characteristics, and root causes of vulnerabilities. The CWE-1000 view spans

1839	   Figure 9 visualizes the distribution of the Top 25 CWE types covered by vulnerable samples
1840	across the selected datasets. Among the mixed datasets and those with a CWE-specific focus,
1841	VulDeePecker, Draper, and SVEN include only a small number of CWEs, i.e., two, four, and nine,
1842	respectively. SecurityEval features the widest variety of CWEs among mixed datasets, with a similar
1843	distribution across its covered types. The CWEs represented in the Top 25 across all datasets
1844	account for only around 20% of its total CWE labels. In comparison, the real-world datasets exhibit
1845	a more pronounced long-tail distribution: the Top 25 CWEs typically account for around 80% of
1846	all vulnerability labels. This highlights a strong skew towards a small set of frequently occurring
1847	vulnerability types.
1848	   The most widely represented CWEs across datasets are those associated with the pillar Improper
1849	Control of a Resource Through its Lifetime, which includes memory and resource management
1850	vulnerabilities that are commonly found in C/C++, the most dominant language across the studied
1851	datasets (cf. discussion in Section 5.1.5). This pillar is also the largest in terms of CWE count (cf.
1852	Table 6), followed by Improper Neutralization, encompassing issues related to input validation and
1853	sanitization. Other pillars are underrepresented in comparison to their relative size in the CWE
1854	view. These pillars include Improper Adherence to Coding Standards and Improper Access Control.
1855	Notably, some pillars, such as Improper Interaction Between Multiple Correctly-Behaving Entities,
1856	Protection Mechanism Failure, and Incorrect Comparison, are not represented at all among the Top
1857	25 CWEs, and are less represented in the overall CWEs covered, cf. Figure 10. These categories
1858	are inherently more difficult to capture in real-world datasets, particularly at the function level, as
1859	they often involve complex inter-component dependencies, system-level interactions, or contextual
1860	analysis that is not easily observable from isolated code snippets.
1861	   A considerable share of CWEs in the analyzed datasets fall into the not mapped category. This is
1862	often the result of outdated or abstract vulnerability labels sourced from the NVD. For instance,
1863	VulDeePecker covers two high-level CWEs, i.e., the class CWE-119 Improper Restriction of Operations
1864	within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer [214] and the category CWE-399 Resource Management
1865	Errors [212], flattening the existing CWE hierarchy and obscuring more specific vulnerability types.
1866	Importantly, the use of abstract categories such as classes for mapping has been discouraged since
1867	2019, as they are frequently misapplied in low-information vulnerability reports where more specific
1868	child CWEs would be more appropriate [214]. The use of categories for vulnerability mapping is
1869	explicitly prohibited [212]. Several other CWEs commonly found in the selected datasets are also
1870	discouraged for use in vulnerability mappings, e.g., CWE-20 Improper Input Validation, CWE-200
1871	Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor, and CWE-400 Uncontrolled Resource
1872	Consumption. In addition, pillars such as CWE-284 Improper Access Control and CWE-703 Improper
1873	Check or Handling of Exceptional Conditions are often used as placeholders in vulnerability reports
1874	lacking detailed analysis, leading to imprecise dataset annotations.

1984	   The use of general or deprecated CWE labels presents challenges to dataset quality and limits
1985	the effectiveness of CWE-based classification and reasoning. Notably, there are 555 CWEs in the
1986	CWE-1000 view that are allowed for vulnerability mapping but are not represented as vulnerable
1987	samples in any of the analyzed datasets. This indicates that current datasets cover only a subset of
1988	CWE types, leaving many mappable software weaknesses absent from training and benchmarking.
1989	As a result, tools trained on these datasets may lack generalization capabilities when faced with
1990	previously unseen vulnerabilities. Further, evaluation results appear artificially strong, as they are
1991	often biased towards commonly occurring CWEs while excluding rare and long-tail vulnerability
1992	types. To address these limitations, more effort is needed to incorporate the CWE hierarchy into
1993	training and evaluation protocols, moving beyond binary labels to consider hierarchically related
1994	CWEs. For example, Tamberg and Bahsi [306] follow an evaluation method in which both parent
1995	and child CWEs are considered valid classifications using MITRE’s Research Concepts view.

1997	5.3             Trends and Use Cases in Dataset Utilization
1998	Understanding how vulnerability datasets are used over time provides insight into community
1999	practices, widely used benchmark datasets, and emerging research directions. Analyzing temporal
2000	trends also reveals how quickly new datasets are adopted, how long benchmark datasets remain
2001	influential, and where gaps or biases may persist in evaluation setups. Such an analysis is partic-
2002	ularly important in this rapidly evolving field to guide future dataset development and advance
2003	performance through more representative and robust evaluations.

2007	serves as a foundational dataset for graph-based and learning-based vulnerability detection models,
2008	and Big-Vul remain in widespread use. Classic test suites such as SARD and Juliet are also frequently
2009	used, cf. Figure 11, useful for controlled evaluations due to their synthetic nature. However, these
2010	earlier datasets often lack current CWE coverage, may reinforce outdated vulnerability mappings,
2011	and may already be part of training corpora.

2123	and model pipelines, and broader community uptake. In many cases, adoption may also depend on
2124	the availability of documentation and preprocessing scripts. Further, early adopters often play a
2125	key role in demonstrating a dataset’s utility, which can influence its acceptance and reuse.
2126	   Another notable trend is the increasing use of newly created or custom datasets, see row "Cus-
2127	tom" in Figure 11. A total of 87 studies either use or introduce custom datasets, often to address
2128	perceived limitations in existing datasets. Common motivations include correcting unrealistic data
2129	distributions, expanding project and vulnerability diversity, including more recent disclosures, or
2130	improving overall dataset quality (e.g., fixing incomplete or incorrectly merged functions) [226].
2131	This trend is also driven by domain-specific or task-aligned needs. While such efforts encourage
2132	innovation and enable tailored evaluations, they also complicate comparability and may introduce
2133	implicit biases tied to individual evaluation design choices and construction assumptions.
2134	   The choice of suitable vulnerability datasets reflects a combination of common benchmark
2135	datasets, task alignment, and system design. However, the use of various datasets across the
2136	surveyed studies illustrates a high degree of fragmentation. Most studies either use or introduce
2137	custom datasets. Only nine datasets are reused in more than ten studies, highlighting the lack of a
2138	standardized suite of benchmark datasets and consistency in dataset selection. Many studies use
2139	more than one dataset, often combining datasets to increase training data diversity or to evaluate
2140	model generalization, e.g., vulnerability types and programming languages. Figure 12 highlights
2141	the most frequently used dataset pairs across all surveyed studies. Among these, the most common
2142	combinations are Devign and ReVeal, Devign and Big-Vul, as well as Big-Vul and ReVeal. These

2343	6     Current Limitations and the Road Ahead
2344	Despite progress in leveraging LLMs for software vulnerability detection, we identified several
2345	remaining limitations in this SLR. In the following, we outline the key limitations derived from the
2346	surveyed studies and propose actionable research directions to address them. Table 7 summarizes
2347	the discussed limitations and future research opportunities.
2348	
2349	6.1    Limitations
2350	The limitations identified in this review emerge from recurring issues observed across the surveyed
2351	studies and span key aspects such as dataset realism and representativeness, vulnerability diversity,
2352	methodological rigor, and evaluation practices. We structure these findings into seven themes
2353	L1-L7 that outline the most pressing limitations.
2354	6.1.1 L1 Dataset and Detection Granularity. In the surveyed studies, vulnerability detection
2355	is typically applied at the level of individual functions or small program slices. This focus on
2356	function-level granularity has been influenced by the dominance of function-level vulnerability
2357	datasets (cf. Table 4) and partly by architectural limitations, particularly the restricted input lengths
2358	of earlier LLMs [293]. However, methods have been proposed to enhance context, such as the work
2359	by Chen et al. [36], and LLMs now support significantly longer input contexts, e.g., 128,000 tokens

2360	for GPT4 [237]. Despite these capabilities, the continued focus on function-level datasets fails to
2361	capture the context necessary to generalize to complex vulnerabilities that span multiple functions
2362	or files. For example, Huynh et al. [119] investigate how varying levels of code context influence
2363	detection performance, comparing snippets enriched with comments and docstrings against full-file
2364	inputs. The findings suggest that even with extended context windows, current models still perform
2365	poorly on distributed vulnerabilities.
2366	   Further, the surveyed studies focus predominantly on detecting vulnerabilities in C/C++code
2367	(cf. Table 5), with limited coverage of other widely used programming languages, such as Java or
2368	Python. This narrow programming language coverage limits the applicability of current models in
2369	diverse, multilingual software environments.
2370	6.1.2 L2 Dataset Labeling and Quality. Synthetic datasets offer high label-precision, as vul-
2371	nerabilities are injected and, thus, well-defined. However, synthetic datasets may oversimplify
2372	real-world scenarios and fail to capture the complexity and diversity of real-world vulnerabilities,
2373	limiting their effectiveness in preparing models for deployment in realistic environments. Similarly,
2374	the common formulation as a binary classification task (cf. Figure 4) lacks the granularity needed
2375	for practical application, where identifying the specific vulnerability type is essential for severity
2376	assessment, prioritization, and appropriate repair. Real-world datasets are typically labeled using
2377	automated methods such as VFCs or static analysis tools. While these approaches enable large-scale
2378	dataset creation, they are associated with label noise and redundancy, which reduce the uniqueness

2432	   Further, most datasets exhibit a strong class imbalance, where vulnerable samples are heavily
2433	outnumbered by non-vulnerable ones (cf. Table 5), and a long-tail distribution of vulnerability types,
2434	with few CWEs dominating and many others being severely underrepresented (cf. Figure 8 and
2435	Figure 9). These imbalances pose significant challenges for both training balance and evaluation
2436	reliability, causing models to overfit to frequent vulnerabilities while failing on rare ones [119].
2437	   Beyond these traditional labeling and quality issues, LLMs introduce the unique challenge of
2438	data leakage. Unlike models trained on closed datasets, LLMs are pre-trained on vast open-source

2450	6.1.3 L3 Study Evaluation and Comparability. The lack of consistency and transparency in
2451	dataset use and evaluation protocols complicates meaningful comparison across studies. Even
2452	within the same use case, studies are often not comparable due to the use of different datasets
2453	(cf. Figure 13). Further, most datasets do not provide predefined train/validate/test splits, which
2454	are essential for ensuring a consistent and fair evaluation [279]. Only a few studied datasets offer
2455	standardized splits, e.g., Draper [267], CodeXGLUE [195] (a subset of Devign [396]), Big-Vul [71],
2456	and PrimeVul [54]. Without fixed splits, results can vary significantly, even when using the same
2457	dataset. For example, if subsequent studies fine-tune on the same dataset but apply different splits,
2458	direct performance comparisons become unreliable. In addition, several studies further modify or
2459	refine existing datasets [91, 113, 338, 369, 378], or augment them with custom data [252]. While
2460	such adaptations are often motivated by practical needs, e.g., improving data quality or evaluating
2461	generalization, they introduce additional variability and complicate comparability with prior and
2462	future works.
2463	6.1.4 L4 Up-to-Date Vulnerability Knowledge. The number of disclosed software vulnera-
2464	bilities continues to grow rapidly [45]. As a result, static datasets may quickly become outdated.
2465	Models trained on such outdated datasets may lack awareness of newly discovered vulnerabilities
2466	and emerging vulnerability patterns, limiting their practical relevance and effectiveness in real-time
2467	scenarios and for the detection of zero-day vulnerabilities [232]. Another challenge lies in how to
2468	efficiently expose models to this growing volume of vulnerability information. Since retraining
2469	models from scratch is computationally expensive and impractical at high frequency, there is a
2470	critical need for scalable methods to update or augment model knowledge.
2471	6.1.5 L5 Code and Vulnerability Representation. In most surveyed studies, the code to be
2472	analyzed is provided as raw code or embedded directly within the prompt during inference. However,
2473	models frequently rely on superficial textual patterns rather than capturing the underlying semantic
2474	structures of vulnerabilities [55, 166, 388]. As a result, model performance degrades under semantic-
2475	preserving code transformations, such as variable renaming, code reordering, or formatting changes,
2476	highlighting a lack of robustness and true semantic understanding [113, 227, 241, 252, 263, 326].
2477	While contrastive learning is designed to produce more discriminative embeddings, models still
2478	often fail to draw the classification boundary correctly and identify the vulnerable patterns [55].
2479	6.1.6 L6 Model Interpretability and Explainability. Current LLM-based vulnerability detec-
2480	tion approaches offer limited insight into why a model classifies the input code as vulnerable or
2481	non-vulnerable. Even in studies that use CoT prompting or explicitly investigate reasoning, issues
2482	with hallucinated or misleading justifications are commonly reported [68, 231]. Similarly, studies
2483	implementing verification report instances of inaccurate corrections, self-contradictions, and hal-
2484	lucinated justifications [373]. These issues undermine the trustworthiness of model outputs and
2485	hinder their integration in practical development workflows where interpretability and reliability
2486	are critical.
2487	6.1.7 L7 Integration into Pipelines and Workflows. Despite growing interest, the integration
2488	of LLM-based vulnerability detection into practical development workflows remains underex-
2489	plored. Only a few studies investigate real-world applicability through prototype tools or user

2506	6.2   Actionable Insights and Future Research Opportunities
2507	Building on the identified limitations, each theme reflects core challenges in current research and
2508	highlights open questions that future work must address to enable more robust, generalizable, and
2509	reproducible progress in LLM-based software vulnerability detection. In this section, we provide
2510	interpretations or promising research directions, offering actionable insights to guide future work
2511	towards addressing these challenges.
2512	6.2.1 L1 Dataset and Detection Granularity. To move beyond the limitations of function-level
2513	detection, future work should focus on context-enhanced vulnerability detection, including project-
2514	and repository-level analysis [99, 172, 345, 394]. Initial steps in this direction include augmenting
2515	function-level samples with additional context, such as surrounding code lines [105], function
2516	arguments, external functions, type definitions, global variables, environmental constraints [264], as
2517	well as dependency and execution flows [391]. For example, Ahmed et al. [3] use GPT-4 to identify
2518	the required contexts for a given vulnerability in a function, but still find limitations in pinpointing
2519	vulnerable statements and their root causes in complex real-world code. Li et al. [169] demonstrate
2520	that incorporating execution and data context improves model performance and reasoning quality,
2521	emphasizing that the challenge lies in precise, context-aware vulnerability reasoning. Similarly,
2522	Yang et al. [364] propose a program analysis-based approach that abstracts complex function calls
2523	into primitive API representations to enrich contextual understanding. Further investigating such
2524	context-enhancements is essential for capturing dependencies that span multiple functions or files,
2525	enabling the detection of more complex vulnerability types that are otherwise missed in isolated,
2526	function-level analysis.
2527	   The current language focus on C/C++ should be expanded to include other widely used languages
2528	such as Python, Java, and Rust [26]. Establishing multilingual and cross-project benchmarks will
2529	be essential for assessing robustness and model generalization.
2530	6.2.2 L2 Dataset Labeling and Quality. To address current limitations in dataset construc-
2531	tion, future work should focus on building real-world vulnerability datasets with improved label
2532	quality and balanced coverage across CWE types. Label quality can be improved through two
2533	main strategies: (1) refining existing datasets via targeted manual labeling to correct and verify
2534	automatically generated labels [111], and (2) advancing automated labeling methods, such as VFCs,
2535	to reduce noise and improve labeling reliability [3, 54, 88, 171, 192]. Balanced coverage across
2536	frequent and less common vulnerability types can be achieved, e.g., by using LLMs to generate
2537	vulnerable samples for specific vulnerability types [19, 275, 370].
2538	   Complementary to improved context, there is a critical need for further reasoning-oriented
2539	benchmarks [301] to close the gap in ground truth. Future dataset creation should prioritize pairing
2540	vulnerable code with verified, step-by-step explanations of the root cause and exploitation logic.
2541	Establishing such reasoning ground truths is a prerequisite for advancing from simple pattern
2542	matching to genuine semantic understanding.

2551	These datasets should set a focus on programming language and vulnerability diversity, capturing

2561	evaluation of test splits) and careful alignment with datasets used in related studies to ensure
2562	meaningful comparisons within the same use case. We provide the mappings of datasets to surveyed
2563	use cases in the artifacts [144].
2564	    To assess generalization and maximize comparability with prior works, models should be eval-
2565	uated on multiple datasets, combining recent datasets such as PrimeVul [54] or MegaVul [226]
2566	with established benchmark datasets such as Devign [396] or Big-Vul [71]. All pre-processing and
2567	filtering steps must be documented to enable replication. In support of open science [233], sharing
2568	of code, evaluation scripts, and model checkpoints is encouraged.
2569	6.2.4 L4 Up-to-Date Vulnerability Knowledge. Given the broad and continuously growing
2570	number of CVEs, ensuring that models remain informed about newly discovered vulnerabilities is
2571	crucial for maintaining relevance in practical scenarios. To address the limitation of static datasets
2572	quickly becoming outdated, future work should focus on continuously maintained and automatically
2573	extensible datasets, such as CVEfixes [21], which employs an automated pipeline for updates.
2574	Advanced adaptation techniques also offer promising pathways to bridge this knowledge gap.
2575	RAG enables LLMs to access external, up-to-date knowledge at inference time. Continual learning
2576	can further support adaptability by integrating new vulnerability knowledge while preserving
2577	performance on previously seen vulnerability types. However, both techniques have seen limited
2578	adoption in the context of software vulnerability detection. Further research should explore their
2579	effectiveness, especially in handling large and heterogeneous vulnerability information. For RAG,
2580	this includes investigating how different representations, e.g., structured CWE hierarchy graphs or
2581	abstract function descriptions, affect retrieval quality and downstream detection accuracy.
2582	6.2.5 L5 Code and Vulnerability Representation. To address the need for robust repre-
2583	sentations that capture vulnerability semantics, future work should further focus on structure-
2584	aware input representations. Directions include graph-based representations, such as control and
2585	data flow graphs, (LLM-generated) abstract descriptions that capture semantics and code behav-
2586	ior [63, 351, 381], and multi-modal inputs, e.g., combining API abstractions, data flow graphs, and
2587	natural language documentation [364]. Understanding how different representations complement
2588	each other can enhance vulnerability detection capabilities. Ideally, such representations should
2589	be language-agnostic to support generalization across diverse programming languages (cf. multi-
2590	language studies [60, 382]). In addition, hybrid architectures should be further explored. GNNs,
2591	in particular, have demonstrated potential for capturing code semantics and structural dependen-
2592	cies [32, 124, 125, 137, 138, 152, 183, 225, 362, 390]. Future work should also evaluate the robustness
2593	of different representation strategies against syntactic perturbations and domain shifts, such as
2594	LLM-generated or refactored code, to better assess real-world generalization capabilities.
2595	
2596	=== [PDF page 42] ===
2597	
2598	42                                                                                       Kaniewski et al.
2599	
2600	
2601	6.2.6 L6 Model Interpretability and Explainability. To build trust in LLM-based vulnerability
2602	detection systems, future research should go beyond standard evaluation metrics (e.g., accuracy,
2603	recall, precision, F1) and incorporate dedicated metrics that assess the trustworthiness and consis-
2604	tency of model-generated explanations. As LLMs increasingly take on roles in security workflows,
2605	their predictions must not only be correct but also justifiable and transparent to developers. Justifi-
2606	cation includes distinguishing between correct predictions made for the wrong reasons (spurious
2607	correlations) and those grounded in valid vulnerability semantics [264]. In this matter, studies
2608	should increasingly look into Explainable AI (XAI) techniques [5, 222, 305].
2609	   Interpretability may further be enhanced through structured explanation formats, such as vulner-
2610	ability propagation paths or flow annotations. These structured rationales offer greater reliability
2611	than natural language justifications and can be cross-checked against program logic or expert
2612	knowledge. Further, integrating RAG techniques with structured vulnerability knowledge, such as
2613	CWE hierarchies or exploit chains, could improve reasoning by anchoring the model’s output in
2614	verifiable context. This approach may not only strengthen the grounding of explanations but also
2615	align with the information needs of developers and auditors in practice.
2616	
2617	6.2.7 L7 Integration into Pipelines and Workflows. To ensure the practical applicability of
2618	LLM-based vulnerability detection, future work should focus on the integration into real-world
2619	development workflows. Such works should, e.g., integrate solutions into IDEs and CI/CD pipelines,
2620	conduct field studies, and collect developer feedback. Closed-source or proprietary codebases can
2621	serve as valuable testbeds for evaluating real-world performance, robustness, and usability.
2622	   Agentic systems and reasoning-driven workflows offer promising pathways to autonomously
2623	assist developers (e.g., expert-in-the-loop system [72]) through tasks such as self-assessment,
2624	explanation generation, or iterative refinement.
2625	   To further improve generalization to practical vulnerability remediation workflows, LLM-based
2626	approaches should move towards CWE-type classification and report generation. Promising direc-
2627	tions include the development of type-specific classifiers that align with the CWE hierarchy and
2628	research views, cf. [14, 25, 51], enabling more actionable insights and effective prioritization.
2629	   A current pathway for industrial adoption lies in synergizing LLMs with traditional program
2630	analysis [159]. While LLMs excel at semantic reasoning, they lack the formal correctness guarantees
2631	of, e.g., formal verification tools. Pipelines where SAST tools detect candidates and LLMs filter false
2632	positives can significantly reduce alert fatigue by applying semantic understanding to noisy static
2633	reports. Conversely, workflows where LLMs propose vulnerabilities and static analyzers verify
2634	feasibility offer a mechanism to ground probabilistic outputs.
2635	   Finally, trade-offs between performance and resource efficiency must be considered for real-
2636	world deployment. Fine-tuning smaller models for on-premise use is both practical and privacy-
2637	preserving [19]. Alternatively, model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation and
2638	quantization offer promising pathways for enabling lightweight deployment on developer machines.
2639	
2640	7    Threats to Validity
2641	To ensure transparency of our findings, we acknowledge potential threats to the validity of this
2642	SLR along with the mitigation strategies employed.
2643	   Paper retrieval omissions. A primary threat to any SLR is the omission of relevant studies
2644	due to studies with incomplete titles, abstracts, or varied keyword terminologies. To address this
2645	threat, we constructed a broad search string based on manually selected keywords from primary
2646	studies as well as keywords from prior SLRs. We combined manual search, automated search, and
2647	snowballing to minimize overlooking relevant papers. Despite these efforts, due to the living nature
2648	
2649	=== [PDF page 43] ===
2650	
2651	A Systematic Literature Review on Detecting Software Vulnerabilities with Large Language Models     43
2652	
2653	
2654	of the field, a static snapshot may miss very recent developments. To address this threat, we employ
2655	a continuous search strategy using alerts and maintain a repository to update the study corpus.
2656	   Study selection bias. The selection of studies involves subjective judgment, which introduces
2657	potential bias. To minimize this threat, we conducted a revision of all crawled papers, strictly
2658	applying predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria (cf. Table 2). A specific threat regarding quality
2659	arises from our decision not to filter exclusively for high-ranked conferences or journals. We
2660	included a wide range of studies to provide a holistic picture of the landscape and identify gaps
2661	that might be missing in a narrower scope. To address the quality implications of this decision,
2662	we provide an analysis of the distribution of studies across conference and journal ranks as a
2663	quality indicator. Additionally, we include preprints from arXiv. While necessary to reflect the
2664	latest advancements, preprints have not undergone rigorous peer review. To mitigate this threat,
2665	we conducted a manual quality assessment, excluding studies that lacked clear evaluation setups
2666	or coherent contributions.
2667	   Data extraction and classification. The manual extraction of information and the construction
2668	of the taxonomy are subject to researcher bias and interpretation errors. For instance, determining
2669	whether a study performs "reasoning" versus "description" can be subjective. To mitigate this risk,
2670	we aligned our taxonomy with existing definitions where possible (e.g., dataset granularity, PEFT
2671	techniques) and refined our categories iteratively during the full-text review. We further support
2672	the reliability of our extraction by publicly releasing the full list of categorized studies and their
2673	attributes in our repository [144].
2674	
2675	
2676	
2677	8   Conclusion
2678	In this SLR, we analyzed 263 studies on LLM-based software vulnerability detection. To structure
2679	this rapidly evolving field, we introduced a comprehensive taxonomy that covers detection task
2680	formulation, i.e., the classification and generation tasks presented to the LLM; input representation,
2681	i.e., how code and auxiliary information are provided to the LLM; system architecture, differentiating
2682	between LLM-centric and hybrid approaches; as well as model adaptation (prompt engineering,
2683	fine-tuning, and learning paradigms) and orchestration techniques, e.g., agentic and ensemble
2684	systems. The analysis shows that most studies perform binary code classification (vulnerable/non-
2685	vulnerable). Common adaptation techniques include full-parameter fine-tuning and zero-shot
2686	prompting. More advanced adaptation techniques, learning paradigms, and orchestration designs,
2687	such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, continual learning, and
2688	agentic workflows, are only beginning to emerge. We further analyzed common datasets used,
2689	investigating their realistic nature, diversity in vulnerability types with respect to CWE-1000
2690	pillars, and usage trends. Despite notable progress in the field, we identified several key limitations
2691	that hinder practical adoption of LLMs in software vulnerability detection, including limited
2692	robustness in code representations, vulnerability data leakage, and limited interpretability and
2693	explainability. To address the identified limitations, we outlined actionable research directions,
2694	such as advancing structure-aware and language-agnostic input representations, aligning datasets
2695	across use cases to enable cross-study comparison and standardized evaluation protocols, adopting
2696	retrieval and continual learning techniques to improve adaptability, and fitting approaches into
2697	practical development workflow requirements. By mapping existing studies, identifying open
2698	challenges, and proposing future research directions, this review aims to guide researchers and
2699	practitioners in advancing the development of reliable, generalizable, and practically applicable
2700	LLM-based vulnerability detection systems.

# Large Language Model for Vulnerability Detection and Repair: Literature Review and the Road Ahead

- Authors: Zhou, Xin; Cao, Sicong; Sun, Xiaobing; Lo, David
- Year / venue: 2025, ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3708522 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3708522
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
- **Version analysed:** arXiv:2404.02525v3 (7 Oct 2024) (p. 1), not the typeset TOSEM version. Numbers or wording may differ slightly from the journal version.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

Convention for this survey: counts about the review's own corpus that appear in its tables/figures are marked [V] (they are the review's own data, although we cannot re-check the underlying extraction). Anything the survey reports about the results of individual primary studies is [A] (second-hand), never [V].

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Provide the first systematic literature review focused on how LLMs are used for source-code vulnerability detection **and** repair, identify limitations of existing studies and propose a research roadmap (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] The authors position it against earlier reviews that covered ML/DL broadly (to 2016, 2020, May 2022) or LLMs for SE in general without detailing vulnerability tasks (p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: What LLMs have been used for vulnerability detection and repair? (p. 5)
- RQ2: How are LLMs adapted for vulnerability detection? (p. 5)
- RQ3: How are LLMs adapted for vulnerability repair? (p. 5)
- RQ4: What are the characteristics of datasets and deployment strategies in these studies? (p. 5)
- No hypotheses; descriptive review.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: SLR "following the guide by Zhang et al." (p. 5). Two search arms: (a) manual search of 13 conferences (ICSE, ESEC/FSE, ASE, ISSTA, CCS, S&P, USENIX Security, NDSS, AAAI, IJCAI, ICML, NIPS, ICLR) and 4 journals (TOSEM, TSE, TDSC, TIFS), yielding 35 papers; (b) automated search of 7 databases yielding 1,500 records; search string derived from the manually found papers (p. 5; Fig. 2, p. 4). Followed by multi-phase screening, quality assessment and forward/backward snowballing (p. 6–7).
- Approach / model / intervention: Descriptive classification (taxonomy) of LLMs (encoder-only, encoder-decoder, decoder-only, following Pan et al.) and of adaptation techniques: fine-tuning (data-centric, program-analysis combination, LLM+other DL modules, domain-specific pre-training, causal learning), prompt engineering (zero-/few-shot), retrieval augmentation (p. 3–4, p. 9–14, Fig. 1 p. 2).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: Not applicable (review). The review does **not** compare LLM approaches with SAST tools or non-LLM DL detectors; GNN/RNN-only studies were explicitly excluded (p. 6).
- Inclusion criteria [A]: English; full text accessible; peer-reviewed full paper in conference/journal (arXiv preprints from 2023–2024 retained subject to quality check); uses LLM techniques for source-code vulnerability detection or repair (p. 5).
- Exclusion criteria [A]: < 5 pages; books, keynotes, technical reports, theses, tool demos, editorials; literature reviews/surveys; duplicates or similar studies by the same authors; no LLM use (e.g. GNN only); LLM only mentioned as future work; not source-code detection/repair (binary code, protocols, network excluded) (p. 5–6).
- Quality assessment [A]: five criteria QAC1–QAC5 (prestigious venue; contribution; clear workflow/implementation; clear experiment details; findings support claims), each scored 0–3, inclusion threshold total ≥ 12 (80%); unpublished preprints scored 0 on venue but kept if total ≥ 12 (p. 6).
- Number of reviewers, independent screening, conflict resolution and inter-rater agreement: not reported.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): manual venue search + IEEE Xplore (197), ACM DL (285), SpringerLink (266), Wiley (205), Web of Science (237), ScienceDirect (220), arXiv (90) (Fig. 2, p. 4) [V].
- Sample size (N) and unit: 58 primary studies (p. 1, p. 7) [V]. Flow: 1,535 records → 1,387 after page filter → 1,332 after de-duplication → 212 after venue/title/abstract → 82 after full text → 42 after quality assessment (37 published + 5 preprints) → +16 from snowballing (83 candidates) = 58 (Fig. 2 p. 4; p. 6–7) [V]. Abstract reports 43 published + 15 preprints (p. 1). Table 2 lists 40 detection studies (p. 10) and Table 3 lists 19 repair studies (p. 16) [V].
- Time window: January 2018 – March 2024 (p. 5); earliest included study is from 2021; 2024 accounts for 46.6% of studies (p. 7) [V].
- Sampling / selection method: see section 3. Snowballing described as "lightweight" (p. 7).
- Data availability: search keywords in an online appendix (Google Doc) (p. 5, ref [8]); extraction sheet and per-study QA scores: not reported.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure: data extraction and analysis section reports only publication-year and venue distribution (p. 7); the extraction form/fields are not reported beyond what is visible in Tables 2–3 (LLM size, adaptation technique, input granularity, data labeling, user interaction, workflow integration) (p. 10, p. 16).
- Code availability: not applicable; online appendix only for keywords (p. 5).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: frequency counts and percentages of LLM usage (e.g. 92 LLM usages in detection, 45 in repair) and of adaptation techniques (p. 7–9, p. 14, p. 17). The review does not aggregate the precision/recall/F1 of primary studies.
- Statistical testing: none (descriptive review). Not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. Encoder-only LLMs dominate detection: CodeBERT is 26.1% (24/92) of LLM usages, GPT-3.5 9.8% (9/92); encoder-only 47.8% (44/92), decoder-only 23.9% (22/92), encoder-decoder 9.8% (9/92), commercial undisclosed 18.5% (17/92) — [V] (p. 7–8)
2. Detection adaptation: fine-tuning ≈73%, prompt engineering ≈17%, retrieval augmentation ≈10% of studies — [V] (p. 9, p. 14). Repair: fine-tuning ≈63%, prompting ≈37% — [V] (p. 14, p. 17)
3. Most detection studies are function-level; only 7 address line-level; no class-level study; one repo-level study ([130] = our `zhou2024comparison`) — [V] (p. 17–18)
4. Detection datasets mostly use heuristic labels (pre-fix functions of vulnerability-fixing commits labelled vulnerable, other functions clean), which prior work showed to be noisy — [A] (p. 18)
5. Repair datasets mostly lack test cases; the two that have them evaluate only 42 and 12 samples — [A] (p. 18)
6. None of the reviewed studies is integrated into developer workflows; all are evaluated offline on static historical data; only one detection study ([113]) produces explanations for developers — [V] (Tables 2–3; p. 19)
7. Only LLM-vs-SAST evidence cited: in [130], "SAST tools achieve low vulnerability detection rates with relatively low false positives, whereas LLMs can detect more vulnerabilities but tend to suffer from high false positive rates" — [A], second-hand from a study by the same first and last authors (p. 22)
8. Best reported state of the art is cited as 67.6% accuracy for detection and 20% for repair (refs [56], [128]) — [A], second-hand (p. 21)
9. LLMs are reported not to be robust to data perturbation ([116], [59]) and to struggle with rare CWE types and inter-procedural / multi-unit vulnerabilities ([51], [84], [128], [129]) — [A] (p. 20–21)

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Only threat to validity discussed: missing relevant studies because of incomplete keywords or varied LLM terminology; mitigated by manual venue selection, automated search and snowballing (p. 24).
- [A] Scope: future versions to add vulnerability localisation and assessment (p. 24).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Dated corpus: search ends March 2024 (p. 5), before most agentic, repository-level and LLM+SAST hybrid work; findings such as "encoder-only dominates" may not hold for 2025-2026 (Kaniewski et al. and Sheng et al. already report decoder-only dominance). Based on the time window and comparison with the other two surveys in this project.
- [I] Very thin evidence on LLM vs SAST: the single repo-level comparison is the authors' own study ([130], Zhou … Lo, 2024, ref list p. 30), so the roadmap claim about SAST vs LLM trade-offs is effectively self-citation, not a synthesis.
- [I] No comparison with non-LLM DL detectors: GNN/RNN-only studies are excluded (p. 6), so the review cannot answer whether LLMs beat DL detectors.
- [I] Quality assessment includes "published in a prestigious venue" (QAC1) as a criterion (p. 6), which mixes venue prestige with methodological quality and structurally penalises preprints.
- [I] Process transparency gaps: number of screeners, agreement and per-study QA scores not reported; the search string is only in an external Google Doc (p. 5).
- [I] Minor internal inconsistencies: the RQ3 answer says "three commonly used techniques" but lists two (p. 17); Limitation 2 opens with "For vulnerability repair" while discussing detection label noise (p. 19); by our count Tables 2 and 3 contain 57 unique study references (Fu et al. [27] and [29] appear in both) versus 58 stated. None changes the main conclusions.
- [I] Repair is half of the scope; detection-specific depth (e.g. metrics, benchmarks, CWE coverage) is limited.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): selection could be biased by the venue-first strategy and the prestige-weighted QA; single-screener vs multi-screener not reported. The review does flag data contamination of LLM pre-training corpora as a concern for primary studies (p. 20).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): corpus limited to Jan 2018–Mar 2024 and source code only (no binaries) (p. 5–6); mostly C/C++ function-level studies (Table 2, p. 10).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): technique shares (≈73/17/10%) are given without a stated denominator (p. 9); classification of studies into categories is not validated.
- Statistical conclusion: not applicable (no quantitative synthesis).
- Reproducibility: keywords in an online appendix (p. 5); extraction data and QA scores not released (not reported).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - Curate a smaller, manually verified, living high-quality test set for vulnerability detection, e.g. by combining manually checked samples from several studies (p. 22).
  - Repository-level detection/repair using long-context LLMs; extend the initial SAST-vs-LLM repo-level comparison (p. 22).
  - Open-source customised LLMs for vulnerability data (p. 22).
  - Unexplored LLM usages: LLM agents, external tool use, advanced RAG (iterative/recursive/adaptive) (p. 22–23).
  - Deployment-ready features: developer interaction, explanations, IDE/VCS integration (p. 23).
  - Benchmarks without overlap with LLM pre-training corpora to avoid data contamination (p. 20).
  - Handle complex vulnerabilities: inter-procedural, rare CWE types, multi-unit vulnerabilities (p. 20).
  - Vision: by 2030, line- to repo-level detection and repair on an expert-annotated benchmark (p. 23).
- Suggested by us [I]: test whether the agent/tool-use and repo-level directions proposed here have since been realised (our corpus contains `guo2025repoaudit`, `li2024iris`, `yildiz2025benchmarking`, `li2026llm`), and whether the SAST-vs-LLM recall/false-positive trade-off reported by `zhou2024comparison` replicates in independent studies.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (dataset labelling, granularity, contamination), RQ5 (limitations and roadmap); marginally RQ1 (one second-hand SAST vs LLM statement) and RQ4 (rare CWEs, inter-procedural vulnerabilities).
- How it informs our work [I]: a peer-reviewed (TOSEM) baseline of the field up to March 2024. Useful mainly to show that (a) as of early 2024 SAST-vs-LLM head-to-head evidence was almost absent, and (b) dataset quality, small input granularity and missing workflow integration were already named as key gaps. Its LLM-vs-SAST statement should be cited to the primary study `zhou2024comparison`, not to this survey.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Only one study in the 58-study corpus compares LLMs with SAST tools (repo-level); it reports SAST tools have low detection rates with low false positives while LLMs detect more but with high false-positive rates (second-hand, same authors' own study) | 18, 22 | A | weak |
| RQ2 | Most LLM detection studies work at function level (7 at line level, 0 at class level, 1 at repo level) | 17–18 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Detection datasets mostly use heuristic labels from vulnerability-fixing commits, shown by prior work to be noisy | 18 | A | moderate |
| RQ2 | Benchmarks may overlap with LLM pre-training corpora (data contamination); contamination-free benchmarks recommended | 20 | A | moderate |
| RQ4 | LLMs reportedly struggle more with less frequent CWE types, inter-procedural and multi-unit vulnerabilities | 20 | A | weak |
| RQ5 | Constructing a high-quality vulnerability detection benchmark remains an open challenge; a curated, living, manually verified test set is proposed | 19, 22 | A | moderate |
| RQ5 | None of the 58 studies is integrated into developer workflows; almost none supports developer interaction/explanations | 19 | V | moderate |
| RQ5 | Under-explored directions (as of Mar 2024): repo-level detection, LLM agents, external tool use, customised vulnerability LLMs | 22–23 | A | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "Constructing a high-quality vulnerability detection benchmark remains an open challenge to date." (p. 19)

> "all studies in our review are not integrated into developers’ workflows and tools but are evaluated only offline using static and historical data" (p. 19)

> "SAST tools achieve low vulnerability detection rates with relatively low false positives, whereas LLMs can detect more vulnerabilities but tend to suffer from high false positive rates" (p. 22)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 24 pages of body text read (abstract to conclusion, Tables 1–3, Figs. 1–8); reference list (p. 24–30) consulted for refs [8], [56], [84], [128]–[130]. Figures 2–8 are partly garbled in the text layer; counts were taken from the text where both exist.
- Version: arXiv v3 (Oct 2024); TOSEM published version (DOI 10.1145/3708522) not compared.
- Uncertainties: denominators of the 73/17/10% technique shares are not stated; mapping of the 43 published + 15 preprint split (abstract) to the 37 + 5 after QA plus 16 snowballed papers is not explained.
- Conflict of interest: funded by the National Research Foundation, Singapore (p. 24). The only SAST-vs-LLM evidence is the authors' own work ([130]).
